#1382. See a tardigrade shed its skin — October’s best science images

The month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’s photo team.

Gonzalo Quiroga Artigas/Nikon Small World

Gonzalo Quiroga Artigas/Nikon Small World

Just another day in space. NASA’s Astrobee, a cubic robot around 30 centimetres across, is designed to work in the microgravity environment inside the International Space Station (ISS). Each of NASA’s three Astrobees — working autonomously, or controlled by ISS astronauts or Earth-bound flight controllers and researchers —  float around taking on tasks such as drawing up inventories and recording experiments. The robots also function as experimental subjects to test microgravity software and hardware.

The Canadian-built arm of the ISS, Canadarm2, holds a Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft during undocking operations. It was released about 420 kilometres above the North Atlantic Ocean on 9 October.

Sting mechanics. A bee’s stinger was observed in action as it injected its venom, called apitoxin, into a gel that mimics skin1. Fiorella Ramirez-Esquivel, a sensory ecologist at the University of New South Wales in Canberra, and her collaborators detached the stinger from a honey bee (Apis mellifera) and studied the mechanics of its pumping mechanism. They discovered that it involves two collapsible cylinders that act as pistons.

Mourning ritual. In northwestern Namibia, Italian photographer Federico Veronesi followed tracks on a dry river bed to catch a rare glimpse of an elephant carrying a dead calf. His shot was the overall winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition, which is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London. Researchers have documented a range of mourning behaviours in African elephants (Loxodonta spp.), including carrying and guarding the dead.

Federico Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Tony Wu/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Tony Wu/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Francisco Negroni/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Francisco Negroni/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

A dung beetle (unidentified species) in Zimbabwe’s Zambezi National Park shot by Oscar Whitfield, who won the Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition.

Photo naturalist Tony Wu spent three years tracking the behaviour of eels off Japan’s southern island of Kyushu. Eventually he captured two specimens of Abbott’s moray eel (Gymnothorax eurostus) in what could be the first photo documenting their spawning behaviour. He used a red light, because the animals spawn at night and are sensitive to other colours of light. On his blog, he wrote that this was “the most difficult and challenging photographic endeavor that I have ever undertaken”.

Nature photographer Agorastos Papatsanis shone ultraviolet light on the forest floor at the foot of Mount Olympus in Greece to reveal the glowing stems of beautiful bonnet mushrooms (Mycena renati). Many fungi fluoresce under UV light — an effect that mycologists can use to help identify species.

Chilean photographer Francisco Negroni took this image of a dead puma (Puma concolor) displayed as a hunting trophy on a fence in the Patagonia region of Argentina.

The Wildlife Photographer of the Year exhibition is on until 11 July 2027 at London’s Natural History Museum.

Beautiful tech. This unusual view, of droplets of ink being squeezed through nozzles and onto paper during the printing process, won first place in the 2026 Nikon Small World competition. Ole Bielfeldt, an experimental photographer in Cologne, Germany, was partially motivated by his desire to understand how inkjet printers work.

Satu Paavonsalo & Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Satu Paavonsalo & Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Dr. Gonzalo Quiroga Artigas/Nikon Small World

Dr. Gonzalo Quiroga Artigas/Nikon Small World

Pierre Nouaux & Laurent Kodjabachian, Camille Boutin/Nikon Small World

Pierre Nouaux & Laurent Kodjabachian, Camille Boutin/Nikon Small World

Brandon Antonio Segura Torres & Priscilla Vieto Bonilla, Paula Alejandra Olivera/Nikon Small World

Brandon Antonio Segura Torres & Priscilla Vieto Bonilla, Paula Alejandra Olivera/Nikon Small World

This mesmerizing web is a cross-section of a mouse eye, showing retinal blood vessels and the optic nerve.

A tardigrade moulting and laying an egg in the old skin.

Skin cells from embryonic Xenopus frogs, show cilia (green), centrioles (a type of organelle, red) and cell membranes (white).

The nuclei in this 20-day-old sea urchin larva fluoresce blue to create a doodle-like outline.

A seal louse (Antarctophthirus sp.) attached to a hair from one of the aquatic mammals.

First responders. Rescuers carry an adult female orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) across a palm-oil plantation in Laman Satong, Indonesian Borneo, on 30 September. Indonesia has been experiencing its worst wildfire season in a decade, blanketing southeast Asia in thick smoke.

Maria D. Guillén/IPHES-CERCA/Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo

Maria D. Guillén/IPHES-CERCA/Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo

Maria D. Guillén/IPHES-CERCA/Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo

Maria D. Guillén/IPHES-CERCA/Antonio Rodríguez-Hidalgo

Neanderthal hand. A dig in a cave in northern Spain has yielded the remains of a 46,000-year-old Neanderthal, including a well-preserved hand. The findings, which were presented in Tarragona, Spain, on 19 October and have not yet been peer reviewed, included analyses of what researchers described as well-preserved ancient DNA.

Space jellyfish. The 13 October launch of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida produced this mesmerizing show as the exhaust glistened in predawn sunlight, and was caught by NASA photographer Bill White. The rocket was headed to the ISS on a resupply mission.

Storm vision. As Typhoon Surigae lingered off the coast of Japan on 28 September, the European Space Agency’s Copernicus Sentinel-1 pictured the sea underneath it using polarized radar. The orange in this false-colour image reveals rough surface conditions caused by strong winds; the calmer seas at the eye of the storm are dark blue.

Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026), processed by ESA

Underwater treasure trove. A stunning 57 new marine species and 5 genera spanning corals, sea cucumbers and crustaceans were identified in just two weeks at an international ‘species discovery’ workshop in Buenos Aires in July. Scientists from across Latin America and Europe gathered to study marine samples, many of which were collected by the deep-sea remotely operated vehicle SuBastian in an expedition led by the Schmidt Ocean Institute to Argentina’s Mar del Plata Canyon in August 2025. The new species include ‘Loki’, a pale sea cucumber with a blob-like body that features two stubby appendages (Peniagone sp.).

#1381. 'I feel betrayed, misled, in shock. It was a stupid thing for them to do': ANDY WOODMAN relives the moment he was 'brutally' sacked by Bromley - and how his best mate Sir Gareth Southgate helped him cope

Published: 21:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 9 November 2026

Every sacked manager has a sob story – but few dismissals have felt as harsh as Bromley’s recent decision to part ways with Andy Woodman.

In his first interview since that decision last month, the 55-year-old tells Daily Mail Sport about feelings of 'betrayal' and 'shock' before making his pitch to future employers. But the most eye-opening part of our candid conversation comes when I ask the man with more than four decades of experience to recall the Bromley Football Club he took over in 2021.

‘Look, Bromley is your classic non-League club,’ says Woodman. ‘I mean that with the greatest respect to all non-League clubs and I hate the word “non-League” as I think it should be “League Three”, as they are all professional.

‘But the facilities are non-League, the mentality is non-League. Everything is done day-to-day, hand-to-mouth, every penny counts, every decision that costs money counts, it is run by people’s personal money.

‘It was tough when I started: we had no turnstiles, no club shop, we trained on the pitch because it was astroturf, we had no gym.’

Under chairman Robin Stanton-Gleaves, Woodman and Co, Bromley changed this mentality and shot up the pyramid, winning the FA Trophy in 2022, promotion to the Football League in 2024 and then another promotion to League One last season.

Andy Woodman was sacked as Bromley boss last month despite leading the club to the FA Trophy in 2022, promotion to the Football League in 2024 and then another promotion to League One last season

Woodman with the FA Trophy in 2022. 'Every manager who gets sacked, we all have a story of hardship to tell and all feel it is unfair,' says the former Bromley boss

Pound for pound, no club has outperformed their history, budget and expectations in English football across the last decade as much as Bromley. But after an understandably tricky start in League One – two wins from their first 10 games – Woodman was sacked.

Asked how he feels about the decision, Woodman, who used to coach in the Arsenal academy system, says: ‘Yeah, I feel betrayed. Every manager who gets sacked, we all have a story of hardship to tell and all feel it is unfair. That’s fine, I get how the football business works.

‘But the bit that didn't sit comfortably with me was the conversations I was having with people at the club or owners, everyone above me… there was no inkling of any of this. I feel misled. I was surprised.

‘One day, we were talking about plans and the way forward and how to get through this sticky little period with players out injured, then the next minute it was a change of direction. Nothing like, “Right, you’ve got three games to turn it round”, none of that, nothing.

‘My record was good there, the owner always said if anyone can churn out results it was myself. Football has no patience. In football, people always forget where they come from. I understand wanting to move forward. It’s disappointing really, that’s the best word I can use. I feel let down.

‘It was just a normal day when they told me. I was going into training, popped across to where the chairman’s office was and then was just told, “We are going to take a change of direction”. It was no more than that, I didn’t try to change the decision or ask why.

‘It was a two-minute conversation, it didn’t need more than that really. I went to tell the staff and went home! It sounds brutal and it is… I am sure people will read this and think, “You deserve this” and “You deserve that” but what else can you do? There’s no easy way of doing it.

'When you have been told you are sacked, you don’t really want to stick around and have a long conversation. They didn’t give an explanation. They needed results, they said. We lost to Leicester which was not a great result, obviously. But realistically they are Leicester… and we are Bromley.’

'It was a two-minute conversation, it didn’t need more than that really. I went to tell the staff and went home! It sounds brutal and it is'

Woodman, who used to be the Arsenal youth team goalkeeping coach, says: 'When I left Bromley that day, I just felt in shock to be really honest'

To hammer home that last point: Woodman’s first game was against Wealdstone in April 2021 in the National League at Hayes Lane. On that same weekend, Leicester were hosting soon-to-be champions Manchester City. Oh, and the Foxes won the FA Cup a month later.

‘When I left that day, I just felt in shock to be honest,’ continues Woodman. ‘I felt the next three games were winnable. I had played seven of the top 10 teams, beaten the top team Huddersfield, my goalie was just coming back from injury and some others were coming back.

‘We had two teams in the bottom four and one just outside so I felt it was my best opportunity to get some much-needed results.

‘To take someone out who has been in football 40 years and been in coaching 25 years and then to put (his former assistant) Byron Webster in charge who had just been fresh out of playing and has never done a coaching session… with every respect, it feels unfair to him. It was a stupid thing to do. I found that really strange, they took one point from those three games. It fascinates me.’

Now, with Bromley bottom of League One, Karl Robinson, the former Salford and MK Dons boss, has taken over. Woodman, though, is keen not to sound bitter and will remember his five-and-a-half years at the club with fondness. He says his best memories are taking Bromley into the Football League, playing at Newcastle in the FA Cup and beating ‘Hollywood Netflix club Wrexham’ in the FA Trophy final.

Sir Gareth Southgate remains his best friend, the pair having met as teenagers in the Crystal Palace academy. They took turns in being best man at each other’s wedding and Southgate is godfather of goalkeeper Andy’s son Freddie, who is on Liverpool’s books.

They also co-authored the 2004 book Woody and Nord which chronicles two polar opposite career paths that started at the same level, one going on to play (and later manage) England, the other a journeyman in the lower leagues.

‘Nothing surprises Gareth and I,’ adds Woodman. ‘We have been in the game for 40 years now. You can argue that in his tenure at England, he got them as high as they have ever been in 60 years and it still was not enough. So it doesn’t surprise us. People have to make decisions and they are business-related, only time will tell if it is the right decision but that’s not my problem any more.

Woodman and lifelong friend Sir Gareth Southgate at the release of their 2004 book 'Woody and Nord' which charts two very different careers in football

Southgate is godfather to Woodman's son Freddie, a goalkeeper on Liverpool's books

‘Gareth was very supportive, so was Alan Pardew and the support from the Premier League right down to the National League, there has been no end of messages I have had, which is comforting.

‘That first Saturday after being out, I didn’t want to be watching or listening to the game, I just wanted to get away because that is the worst. I have had two clubs ring me, there are ongoing conversations and I am just making sure it is the right vehicle for me. What I mean by that is I want an owner that is aligned and who thinks they can compete to get out of their league.

‘My record speaks for itself. If you ask most managers how many promotions and trophies they have won, I bet over long careers, they haven’t got many. For me, with the smallest budget in the leagues, we maximised the team and maximised success.

‘To get two promotions and an FA Trophy win against Wrexham, hitting the play-offs four times in five years, that is something I am really proud of. If nothing else, the Bromley supporters and town are grateful.’

#1379. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

Jacquet goes into the book. A loose pass out from the back is picked off my Brentford substitute Schade and Jacquet snaps in too enthusiastically and receives a yellow.

Chance! Will Fulham rue all these missed chances? King is involved once more, standing up a cross to the back post where Garcia nods down for Iwobi to stroke goalwards near the penalty spot, but Tzolakis does well to get down low to his left and keep Fulham’s advantage to just one goal.

Mateo Kovacic comes off injured for City. It is probably just a knock as he’s sat on the bench rather than heading down the tunnel. Was a standout player in the first half.

Close! Ajayi’s clearance comes straight back and Charles works the ball to King on the right, but with just the keeper to beat, the midfielder’s effort is saved by Tzolakis with his feet. King really should be scoring there.

Still some time before the Liverpool game resumes given the time added on at the end of the first half.

Following his clash of heads with Jarrad Branthwaite in the lunchtime kick-off at the Hill Dickinson Stadium, the Chelsea goalkeeper has now been taken to hospital to undergo precautionary tests.

Brentford lead Liverpool thanks to Keane Lewis-Potter's header, but the second half could be tricky for the Bees after Yehor Yarmoliuk was sent off just before half-time. Liverpool are yet to have a shot on target despite having seven shots in the first half. #BRELIV https://t.co/o9HE2Fh8qb

Andrews will be furious with how that first half ended. His side had done brilliantly to establish a lead, but will have their work cut out keeping Liverpool out after the break with the visitors a man to the good.

With half-time fast approaching and Brentford in front, this is absolute madness. Yarmoliuk looks to have butted Jacquet in an incident that reminds of Bentacur’s red card at Old Trafford last weekend.

The referee is sent to the pitchside monitor after a lengthy delay and Yarmoliuk is off!

We’ve had the second VAR review in just a few minutes here, and this one has resulted in a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk for a “headbutting action”. I have to say, this feels harsh. It’s pretty tame. There is a tiny movement towards Jacquet, who collapsed to the turf in dramatic fashion, but he’s hardly caused the Liverpool defender any damage. That will change the dynamic of this game.

Haaland restores City’s lead after Maeda had cancelled out Foden’s opener.

Arbeloa’s side are in front and could have been ahead by a wider margin, but we’ve been here before...

Gary Neville is a w-----, is a w-----.....is quite a loud chant here at City. Fans in a good mood here after Erling Haaland scored in his eighth game in a row.

Brentford 1 Liverpool 0 (Lewis-Potter) Outtara curls in a wonderful cross and Lewis-Potter steals in to head the ball beyond Alisson from 10 yards out.

Brentford take the lead, and it’s a lead they probably just about deserve on the run of play. It’s an absolutely superb header by Keane Lewis-Potter, up from left-back, as he thumps Igor Thiago’s cross into the top corner of Liverpool’s net. Textbook technique.

Just after Wirtz was denied a penalty of his own, Mac Allister looks to have won a spot-kick for real off a challenge from Outtara. The referee gives it, but is then sent to the monitor and the decision is reversed. Correct decision. Outtara clearly got a piece of the ball first.

Liverpool have been awarded a penalty but I don’t think this will stand. It shouldn’t stand. Dango Ouattara got a touch on the ball when he lunged in on Alexis Mac Allister.

Yep, the penalty has been overturned. Referee John Brooks missed Outtara’s touch on first viewing but the replays were pretty conclusive.

Manchester City 2 Ipswich Town 1 (Haaland) Kovacic wriggles free of his markers and darts to the by-line. He’s able to stand up a cross and Haaland heads the ball forcefully downwards - just as your grassroots football coach always told you to - and Walton is unable to keep it out. Probably should have done better.

Fulham 1 Hull City 0 (Iwobi) A big, big goal for Fulham and Arbeloa. They are finally able to convert their overwhelming dominance with the ball into something material. This goal comes at the end of a sweeping move, with Iwobi stroking the ball beyond Tzolakis, who probably should have done better.

Bradley Barcola may not be justifying his fee at Liverpool yet but another Frenchman, Jeremy Jacquet, certainly is. The centre-back has been excellent all season and he has just produced a goal-saving challenge on Brentford’s Igor Thiago. A sliding tackle, perfectly timed, just as Thiago was about to score.

Brentford are getting the ball forward quickly, and Kelleher is the one to initiate the latest move. He finds Thiago on the halfway line, who gets the ball back off Outtara, but the Brazilian’s effort is well blocked by Van Dijk.

Some bad news for Liverpool, though, as Szoboszlai sits on the turf. It looks like his afternoon might already be over.

Daizen Maeda showed good strength to hold off Marc Guehi’s challenge before scoring his first goal for Ipswich since signing from Celtic. City will be disappointed with the defending there - it was a straightforward ball down the channel from Abdoul Ouattara.

Before that Phil Foden sent a message to Thomas Tuchel with the opening goal. Foden, playing in central midfield, was left out of the last England squad and has seen Alex Scott climb above him in the pecking order. But Scott is injured for next month’s international which may give Foden a chance.

Was Bradley Barcola’s midweek hat-trick the start of a great run of form for the £123m forward? Not on this evidence. A defensive mix-up allowed the Frenchman a clear run at goal, one-on-one with Brentford’s Caoimhin Kelleher, but his finish was woeful. An attempted dink that bobbled harmlessly wide. “What a waste of money,” comes the cry from the Brentford fans.

Manchester City 1 Ipswich Town 1 (Maeda) Woah, barely a minute between these two goals at the Etihad. Guehi relinquishes possession to Maeda and, left alone in the box, he stears the ball into the far bottom corner.

Manchester City 1 Ipswich Town 0 (Foden) While Foden has scored, huge credit must go to Doku, who did brilliantly down the left, working the ball on to his right foot before squaring to Foden who gets a shot away - Walton does well to get a hand on the ball, but he cannot keep it out.

“You’re going down with the City,” sing the home fans at the Ipswich travelling support.

Bright start by Brentford here, although Liverpool have just created their first chance of the game as Szoboszlai shoots over from the edge of the box.

Liverpool break and their sweeping move up the field comes to Wirtz whose cut-back picks out Szoboszlai perfectly but the midfielder miscues and his effort does not trouble Kelleher.

Ipswich centre-back Issa Diop did not take the knee like the other players on the pitch just before kick-off here at the Etihad Stadium. The Premier League’s ‘No Room For Racism’ initiative is this weekend and players have been invited to kneel on the pitch. Fulham simply need to win today and they get off to a good start. Iwobi goes close with an early effort which is turned behind by Tzolakis.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1378. Tom Brady QUITS Birmingham City just three years after investing in the club - with Blues top of the Championship

Published: 16:22 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 21:57 EST, 9 November 2026

Tom Brady has sensationally quit Birmingham City just three years after becoming involved with the Championship club.

The Blues said in a statement, released Monday night: 'Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years.

'It was amazing to have someone with Tom's experience and passion associated with the club, and the club looks forward to continuing on that foundation from the training ground to the Birmingham community.'

The NFL icon joined Birmingham City as a minority investor as part of a takeover spearheaded by billionaire Tom Wagner's Knighthead Capital in the summer of 2023.

Brady's presence in the English football pyramid was heralded with a five-part documentary on the new ownership's plan to revamp the Midlands club, titled: 'Built in Birmingham: Brady and the Blues'.

Within the five-part Amazon series, Brady notably lambasted Wayne Rooney for his work ethic after installing him briefly in the dugout after despatching previous head coach John Eustace.

Tom Brady (right) has quit Birmingham City just three years after his investment in the club

The NFL legend became a minority owner three years ago but has now called it quits

The fly-on-the-wall documentary showed Brady visiting the Birmingham training ground to observe Rooney's team meeting and training session. While driving away, he tells his business manager Ben Rawitz: 'I'm a little worried about our head coach's work ethic.'

Rawitz replies: 'Comes across as lackadaisical.' Rooney was sacked after 83 days in charge.

The documentary later saw Brady admit his error in replacing Eustace with the former England international and reveal that he was warned against making 'sweeping changes' so early in his time with the club.

'I had good advice, "Don’t go in there and make sweeping changes. You guys have time",' said Brady. 'But we made sweeping changes that put us in decline. That was our doing.'

Under the aegis of Brady and Knighthead Capital, Birmingham City have launched what the group see as a 20-year megaproject, with £3billion earmarked for investment in a 'Sports Quarter' in the city.

The 48-acre site in the east of the city is set to feature a new 60,000-seater stadium and training ground above a network of underground transport tunnels.

But since the plan was announced, there have been some wrinkles with the timeline – pushing the stadium's completion deadline from 2029 to 2031.

Daily Mail Sport understands that London-based architects Heatherwick Studio – in conjunction with Kansas City-based Manica – are set to work on a design with a 'chimney theme' in a nod to the city's industrial heritage.

He infamously hired Wayne Rooney as manager, before the former England captain was sacked 83 days later

Peaky Blinders creator and famous Bluenose Steven Knight is believed to be working with the team to ensure it is 'one of the most-talked about stadium designs ever'.

Last season, Brady had promised promotion to the Premier League. The club are top of the Championship going into the last international break of the year, though he has departed before they can reach the top flight again.

Brady's involvement had been lauded by Wagner, and his departure was met with a mixed reaction by fans on social media.

One wrote on X: 'Didn't contribute anything after the first season, good riddance.'

Another wrote: 'What did he even do? Even his fitness guy didn't contribute anything, we had more injuries than ever.

'PR stunt, better off without him being involved. Embarrassed us on the Amazon doc too.'

A third, though, posted: 'Some of these clueless comments. He's a brand name and he made us globally talked about, globally looked at, globally listened to.

#1375. Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The abandonment of villages in Japan is changing ecosystems. Studies are finding that biodiversity has declined in places that people have left behind.Credit: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Bloomberg/Getty

The idea that humanity is separate from the rest of the planet is deep-rooted, but wrong. Indeed, for most of human history, this has not been the case1. Many landscapes seen by European colonists as ‘wilderness’ were in fact tended by Indigenous people. This includes North America’s wildflower-studded oak savannahs and Australia’s fire-maintained ecosystems. Worldwide, traditional agricultural practices — which have been used for millennia, in some cases2 — have created ecological niches that support insects, amphibians, birds and plants, many of which have evolved together with humans.

When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn

When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn

People have always cleared land to some extent. But the scale of this practice has been unprecedented since the beginning of industrialization in the mid-eighteenth century, and especially since the onset of industrial farming. Intensive land conversion is the biggest driver of biodiversity loss. It’s a key reason why countries agreed four years ago to protect 30% of land and water habitats by 2030 (also called the 30 × 30 target).

That goal, however, explicitly did not intend for protected areas to be human-free zones3. Now, as Nature reports in a News feature, evidence is emerging that biodiversity does not necessarily thrive in places that humans leave behind. In Japan, where entire villages are being abandoned because of rural depopulation, the decline in traditional rice-farming practices and woodland management is reducing habitat availability for many birds, insects and plants that thrive in flooded paddies, along field margins or in open-canopy forests.

This example and others show that protected areas need humans to be responsible for specific tasks. These jobs include water management, the provision of grazing animals and ecologically informed forestry, such as using prescribed burning to prevent catastrophic megafires similar to those the world is seeing increasingly. The Americas, Europe and Australia will need many thousands of fire-trained professionals in the coming decades.

Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity

Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity

Land-tending practices also include traditional foraging and planting, the building of clam gardens on the coast and cutting down trees and shrubs to thin woodlands and stimulate fresh growth. Such work must be informed by modern ecology and conservation biology — which increasingly incorporate lessons from ecological knowledge that comes from, in some cases, millennia of practical field experiments.

These practices also need to be funded. Traditional farming and land-management techniques are expensive compared with industrial agriculture, which requires less labour and has huge yields. If humanity wants to preserve these traditional relationships with the planet and the biodiversity they support, governments will have to subsidize this work directly.

This is already being done in a limited way, through grants to farmers and in agricultural-biodiversity schemes. However, nations should consider providing robust and comprehensive support. Programmes could be based on the US Civilian Conservation Corps — created during the Great Depression in the 1930s — although standards would need to be updated to improve diversity and equity, and activities would have to be supported by evidence.

Biodiversity conservation has an evidence problem — it’s time to fix it

Biodiversity conservation has an evidence problem — it’s time to fix it

At a time of mass unemployment in the private sector, the corps was a publicly funded job-creation scheme that employed three million young men. Working in teams, they planted trees, prepared terraced fields, built roads and trails, erected fire towers and otherwise tended to US natural resources between 1933 and 1942.

Today, artificial intelligence is raising concerns not only about its environmental impacts4, but also that it could cause another phase of high levels of unemployment. Governments looking to establish schemes that could buffer their workforces against job losses associated with technological changes should consider investing in people’s relationships with land, water and biodiversity. It would be a mutually beneficial outcome: for people and the ecosystems we inhabit.

#1374. Brilliant Blues Earn Solid Point Against Title-Contenders Chelsea

Everton earned a brilliant point against title-chasing Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday afternoon.

The hosts opened the scoring on 28 minutes via Melvine Malard, but the resilient Blues showed real character to restore parity only five minutes later as Yuka Momiki's in-swinging cross took a deflection off former-Toffee Lucy Bronze.

The result follows another terrific point claimed last week – Scott Phelan's side drawing against high-flying Manchester United at Goodison Park on Sunday.

Head coach Phelan named an unchanged XI from the side that claimed that solid stalemate against the Red Devils on Halloween.

It was the hosts who threatened first as Ellie Carpenter commenced one of her trademark bursts down the right. Upon breaching the box, she pulled the trigger from a narrow angle. Rion Ishikawa did well to track her run and block her effort, the ball hitting the side-netting.

Moments later, Malard was inches away from opening the scoring. The French forward ghosted to the back-post and seemed destined to head home from point-blank range. Fortunately, the striker misjudged the trajectory of the ball and subsequently missed the target.

Chelsea’s number nine made no mistake when presented with a second opportunity, though. Bronze headed McCabe’s clipped cross back across the face of goal, where Malard converted on 28 minutes.

The Toffees levelled only five minutes later, though, as Momiki’s dangerous ball from the left struck the boot of full-back Bronze and nestled in to the bottom left corner.

Then, the England international was in the thick of the action once more at the other end as her header rattled the crossbar five minutes later.

That concluded the action for the opening 45, with the Blues first to register an attempt following the interval. Hikaru Kitagawa sprinted down the left before sending a lofted cross in to the area. Pacheco did well to latch on to it, but could only glance agonisingly wide.

Vignola was next to try her luck after cutting-in from the left deep in to the second half. The forward’s strike whistled just wide of the far-post, with Hannah Hampton rooted to the spot.

The hosts responded as Walsh rifled an effort in to the palms of the diving Brosnan with 15 to go.

Phelan made his first change of the game with six minutes remaining as Momiki made way for Noemie Mouchon.

Galli then replaced the tireless van Gool with 90 minutes on the clock.

After four minutes of injury time, the referee concluded the clash to mark an excellent point on the board.

Next, Phelan’s side look to make it four wins from four in the Subway Players Cup on Wednesday night (7pm KO) as Durham travel to Goodison Park.

By DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 21:47 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 23:51 EST, 9 November 2026

US soccer fans were sent into a frenzy on Monday by the news that Mauricio Pochettino is in pole position to join Manchester United.

As reported by the Daily Mail, Michael Carrick is facing the sack with United bosses leaning towards hiring a new coach during the international break.

Pochettino has emerged as a frontrunner for the role, despite signing a new contract following the World Cup, when he led the USMNT to the last 16.

The Argentine committed his future to the end of the next World Cup in 2030 but his contract includes a £7 million ($9.4 million) release clause. And news of Manchester United's interest left many USMNT fans fearing the worst.

'[That] was fun while it lasted!' one said. 'Wow - just when you thought things had settled a bit with the USMNT!' added a second, while a third said: 'Noooo they can’t have our coach!'

Many other supporters on social media refused to believe that Pochettino could leave but his future has been under the microscope ever since he took over in September 2024.

Mauricio Pochettino is in pole position to replace Michael Carrick at Manchester United

Carrick is facing the sack with United leaning towards hiring a new coach in the coming weeks

The 54-year-old Pochettino has made no secret of his desire to return to the Premier League

The 54-year-old has made no secret of his desire to return to the Premier League, while it emerged ahead of the World Cup that he had held discussions with AC Milan.

Pochettino's team sparkled en route to the last 16, only to crash out against Belgium after President Trump's intervention over the red card shown to striker Folarin Balogun.

His initial contract expired after the tournament but after weeks of uncertainty, the former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton coach signed a four-year extension.

He is slated to take charge of a Nations League double-header against Haiti during this international break, with a press conference set for Friday.

Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann, who were both under consideration when United gave Carrick more time to turn the season around following a 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth last month, could also be in contention.

#1372. Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

It is getting hard to comprehend what Jaissle wants his team to do. The much-hyped “vertical” style looks like an ugly incarnation of the long ball football of yesteryear. They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. They did not have a shot on target in the first half and, other than one fantastic save in the second, Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki had nothing to do.

"If he doesn't slip Harvey Barnes in, he's got to hit the target" Shay Given discusses Newcastle's decision-making in the final third 🔲 https://t.co/wh4kCAEbxV

“Our decision-making in the final third was lacking today,” Jaissle said. “I am frustrated, I understand the supporters’ reaction, that is their right [to boo after a defeat at home].”

It is time for a sharp dose of medicine on Tyneside. Expectations need to be adjusted, especially as none of the new signings have impressed. This was always the fear and the risk when you put all your faith in young players from abroad.

For Jaissle’s vertical football to work, Newcastle need to be able to win the ball high up the pitch, whether that is with a high press or competing for second balls from long passes. They do not do either well. More worryingly, they look so vulnerable, so easy to play through.

Villa did it to them all afternoon. Nicolas Jackson should have scored in the first half, Ibrahim Mbaye should have hit the target in the second.

On another day, Newcastle could also have had centre-back Sven Botman sent off for a lunge on Jackson. Then it really would have become ugly, but the Dutchman survived a VAR check.

Villa were always the better side. There was no fluency in Newcastle’s game, no structure, no patterns of play. Every time they turned over the ball, they looked stretched. Every time they got a set-piece, it was defended easily. Every time they went forward in the first half, the ball was sent aimlessly long and came straight back at them. In the second, they huffed and puffed but did not sustain any pressure on the Villa goal. The missed chances late on were not clear opportunities and they were snatched at by the hapless Yoane Wissa.

Yoane Wissa fails to hit the target after an inspiring run! ❌ https://t.co/ohabzLZBRv

It was largely poor and so was the manner in which Villa took the lead. João Gomes was given the time and space to loft a cross to the far post for Manzambi, who had drifted away from Lewis Miley, to head home.

Newcastle were in disarray and it should have been 2-0 almost immediately when Emiliano Buendía received the ball in the middle of the area and crashed a shot against a post.

The home crowd tried to remain patient and supportive, but the sight of yet another long, aimless ball being punted forward straight to a Villa defender tipped some over the edge. There were boos and jeers in the stands while Jaissle screamed at Joe Willock and Wissa. There were more boos at half-time; things felt combustible.

Newcastle needed a big second half. They were better, but it was hardly anything to get excited about. A shot on the turn from Botman, superbly saved by Suzuki. Then a few half-chances were squandered, the occasional flash of a threat and that was it.

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Villa man said: “It was a difficult game. St James’ Park is always very difficult to play in. Very happy we got the three points and very happy to win here.”

When asked about the Botman challenge in the first half, he replied: “The referee said it was a yellow card but it was so high. Hopefully next time it is a red card. I nearly broke my leg, but it’s fine. It’s part of football.”

Villa move up to 12th, level on points with Newcastle in 11th, who have now lost three of their last four Premier League games. There’s questions for Jaissle, while Villa are beginning to gather momentum this season under Emery after a slow start.

A Newcastle cross causes chaos in the Villa box, with Mings heroically hooking the loose ball away. That could do it for Villa, who are seconds away from the three points.

Jackson can’t make the most of the latest Villa break, with Hall and Thiaw defending well. Burn is quite literally playing everywhere, popping in numerous areas across the pitch. Still, a goal eludes Newcastle.

Burn is playing as a makeshift striker. The game has descended into a free-for-all from a Newcastle perspective.

Mbaye goes close again! The winger skips away from Miley and darts into the box, before dragging a low strike narrowly wide of the bottom corner. Manzambi is down and in need of treatment. Gonzalez hurriedly goes over to try and help the Villa man, but Manzambi isn’t interested. A triple change for the visitors is imminent.

Miley’s searching cross is headed away by Lindelof but only as far as Wissa. The former Brentford man attempts an acrobatic volley, only to see it blocked by a couple of Villa bodies.

Villa are retreating deep, inviting Newcastle to put them under some pressure. However, the hosts are lacking attacking invention and threat, with Villa’s lead still looking relatively safe.

Miley clips in a cross and Wissa wins the header. The striker directs his looping attempt over the bar. It won’t classify as a chance, but it’s more encouraging from Newcastle.

Wan-Bissaka tracks back excellently to defend against Toure before getting his body in front of the ball to win a foul. It’s another decision met by furious boos from the home fans.

A double switch 🔄 Come on, lads! 💪 [0-1] 57' https://t.co/ysiribFvcI

Wissa closes down Suzuki and the striker catches the goalkeeper. There’s no malice in challenge, but the Newcastle man is booked. Safe to say that the majority of St James’ Park don’t agree with the decision.

Gonzalez cynically pulls McGinn back as the Villa captain glides away from the Newcastle midfielder, who picks up a yellow card.

That Botman shot was by far the closest Newcastle have come to scoring so far. The home fans will hope they can continue to put Villa under pressure.

Botman tests Suzuki! Villa fail to clear a Newcastle free kick and the ball breaks to Botman, who swivels and powers a first-time effort at goal. The venomous strike forces Suzuki into a brilliant diving save. Botman scored a stunner at Coventry on Monday and saw his names in lights again, but Suzuki was there to deny him.

We are back under way for the second half. Villa have made a half-time alteration, with McGinn replacing Alysson, who was booked in the first half, while Newcastle are unchanged.

Another dreadful half for Newcastle United and the home fans are getting increasingly exasperated with Matthias Jaissle’s tactics. The aimless long balls pumped forward for nobody to reach, and which normally go straight to an Aston Villa defender, have drawn boos. There were more at the half-time whistle. Whatever the plan is, it isn’t working and it has not for weeks. A pattern is emerging, and it is really worrying for Newcastle. They look like a disorganised mess.

#NEWAVL – 17' The referee's call of yellow card to Botman for the challenge on Jackson was checked and confirmed by VAR. REF: "I think it's reckless. Even though you get a touch on the ball, it's still reckless".

Villa have been the better side and deservedly lead Newcastle 1-0 at St James’ Park thanks to Manzambi’s header. The visitors look so dangerous on the break in forward areas, while the hosts are struggling at the back. Botman was also lucky to escape a red card following a VAR review of his forceful challenge on Jackson. There’s a lot for Jaissle to ponder as he attempts to plot a route back into this contest for Newcastle. Emery’s game plan has worked wonders.

More of that in the second half, please 😮‍💨 https://t.co/nZ6mBuXKQF

There will be two minutes of added time. Could Villa add a second goal before the break?

Each time Villa burst forward they look like they could score. On this occasion, Manzambi and Jackson combine, but the latter can’t quite take the ball under his spell, allowing Gonzalez to track back and recover.

Villa hit the post and Newcastle all over the place at the back! Jackson is released and pulls a cross back to Buendia, who agonisingly places an effort against the inside of the post. It hits Hornicek’s back as he dives. That could have gone anywhere. Villa are looking dangerous and the Newcastle fans are starting to become very restless.

Shocking defending from Newcastle! There’s no pressure on Joao Gomes, who’s allowed to float a cross into the box. Manzambi peels away from Miley, before directing an unchallenged header into the net.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

Buendia chips a pass through for Alysson to chase. Hornicek dashes out of his box to head it away and Alysson accidentally bumps into him. The home crowd scream for a card, with Alysson already on a yellow, but there’s absolutely nothing in the challenge, with VAR checking it very quickly.

All pretty one dimensional from Newcastle so far with nothing to really hurt Aston Villa in their attacking play, but the VAR check for a red card on Sven Botman has woken the crowd up. The Villa coaching staff and players were appealing for a red which incensed Newcastle and their supporters. It was an ugly challenge from Botman and he did have two feet in the air but he did not connect with Jackson with his studs and won the ball with his backside in the end.

The ball is overturned and Manzambi feeds Jackson, who has pulled out into the attacking left channel. He tries to bend an effort into the far bottom corner, but it’s bloked by Botman.

You guessed it, there’s another yellow card. This time, Alysson is booked for simulation as he runs into traffic. It’s a very theatrical dive. There was no contact from Joelinton.

Joao Gomes is the next player to go into the book after he pulls Fernandez-Pardo’s shirt. The decision is met by ironic cheers from the home crowd. The Villa midfielder tries to protest against the decision and Buendia has to push him away to stop him from talking his way into a second yellow.

It’s been a feisty game so far. Newcastle fans are unhappy with the number of fouls given against them. The hosts are being very aggressive with their press as Gonzalez dispossesses Kamara to force a corner, but nothing comes from the set piece.

Newcastle fans can breathe a huge sigh of relief as Botman’s card stays as a yellow. The defender is a very lucky man.

Referee Gillett shows two yellow cards in incredibly quick succession as Joelinton and Botman both fly into forceful challenges on Manzambi and Jackson respectively. The crowd furiously boo both decisions. Botman’s tackle on Jackson was wild and over the top of the ball, with VAR checking for a possible red card.

Villa are finding holes in Newcastle’s defence as Manzambi plays in Cash, who fires into the side netting from a tight angle. Emery and his players are convinced they should of had a corner.

Once again, Villa hit Newcastle on the counter. This time, Jackson turns provider and tries to thread a pass into Alysson’s path. However, Hall is on high alert and defends diligently to intercept and clear.

Huge chance for Villa! Out of nowhere, Villa counter from a Newcastle corner. It’s excellent play from Alysson, who powers past his marker before slipping a pass to the onrushing Jackson. The striker is through and chops inside of Botman, before shooting straight at Hornicek with the outside of his boot. Given the ruthless form he’s been in, you’d expect more from Jackson there.

Villa are penned in at the moment, with Newcastle having made a fast start in these early stages. Suzuki has the ball and he’s put under tremendous pressure from Wissa. The goalkeeper is calmness personified as he coolly passes to Cash.

Fernandez-Pardo drives at Wan-Bissaka and tries to find Willock with a low delivery. The cross is intercepted by Lindelof, but it’s positive play from Newcastle’s summer recruit, who is lining up in his preferred position out wide.

Early signs reveal that Fernandez-Pardo is playing on the right wing, with Wissa operating as the central striker and Willock pushed up as the most advanced midfielder. Barnes is on the left.

Villa get us under way at St James’ Park.

Both line-ups are out on the pitch. St James’ Park is absolutely buzzing as the Premier League anthem rings around the stadium after a modified edition of Blaydon Races, with kick-off minutes away.

There is a new version of the Blaydon Races, reworked by Newcastle United in order to become their club’s official pre-match anthem. It is slower than the original and lacks a bit of oomph. But, you know what, I wanted to hate it and it was actually okay. Once supporters get used to the new pace of the song they should start joining in with the singing. I have to constantly have to remind myself at this age that just because something is new and different doesn’t mean it is bad.

Newcastle will be relieved that this game is at St James’ Park, with the club having lost their previous two away fixtures 4-1 against both Coventry and Leeds.

Summer signing Nicolas Jackson has five goals in his previous six games for Aston Villa in all competitions and looks to be brimming with confidence as he leads the line for Unai Emery. The striker dispatched both finishes for his brace against Fenerbahce with unerring composure and will target more goals at St James’ Park.

One of the interesting subplots to this evening’s game will be watching Johan Manzambi playing for Aston Villa.

The Switzerland international’s decision to reject Newcastle in order to sign for Villa helped convince Eddie Howe to quit in the summer.

Having already missed out on Victor Munoz, who decided to join Liverpool at the last moment, losing Manzambi - their first-choice target across the position board - was a blow Howe did not feel he could recover from.

In short, he was not convinced the alternatives would give him the tools to do the job this season. Aladji Bamba, who was signed instead, has not started a game for Newcastle this season and appears to be well down the pecking order in the centre midfield under Howe’s successor Matthias Jaissle.

Manzambi had a slow start to his Villa career because of injury but he was hugely impressive at the World Cup for Switzerland and is expected to become one of the best midfield players in Europe over the next few years. Nobody can say with any degree of confidence that will be the same for Bamba.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage as Newcastle United welcome Aston Villa to St James’ Park in the Premier League.

Newcastle endured a hellish Monday night as they were condemned to an embarrassing 4-1 defeat by Coventry City in their previous top-flight outing. Matthias Jaissle’s rebranded Newcastle outfit have notably lacked consistency in the early weeks of the season, with the loss to Coventry another abrupt reminder of how this is expected to be a challenging campaign for his freshly assembled squad. The new arrivals are yet to fully settle and Newcastle are undoubtedly still adapting following a turbulent summer transfer window where they lost several key players.

Meanwhile, Villa arrive up north in tremendously high spirits following their 6-0 thumping of Fenerbahce in midweek Champions League action, thereby recording their biggest European win in the club’s history. However, in a similar vein to Newcastle, Villa have struggled to impose themselves in the Premier League, triumphing just once in their opening six matches of the season. Unai Emery’s men conceded a 79th-minute equaliser to Brentford’s Kristoffer Ajer last time out in the Premier League to draw 2-2 and deepen their domestic frustration.

Despite how this week’s results have shaped contrasting moods in the two camps, Newcastle are currently three points ahead of Villa in the Premier League, with today’s visitors aiming to make it back-to-back top-flight away wins after beating Tottenham 3-2 in the capital last month.

Jaissle is still trying to find his feet in English football, and hosting Villa is yet another tough test of his credentials. Meanwhile, it’s a question of when Emery’s new-look Villa will click, not if, given his unbelievable impact at the club. The Spaniard is fast approaching his four-year anniversary as Villa’s head coach, and what a journey it has been.

We’ll bring you all the latest updates and drama from Tyneside. Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1369. Academy Graduate Tom Davies Features In Under-21s Game

Academy graduate Tom Davies will feature in Everton Under-21s' Premier League 2 clash away to Crystal Palace on Sunday, as the Academy continues to support the midfielder with his fitness as he looks to secure a professional contract elsewhere.

Davies – a free agent after leaving Sheffield United at the end of last season – has been training with the Under-21s to support the Blues' younger players while building his own fitness.

Davies, who will start on the bench this afternoon, joined Everton Academy at the age of 11 and developed through the age groups before making his Men’s debut aged 17 in April 2016.

The boyhood Blue became the youngest captain in Everton’s history when he skippered the side, aged 20, for a 2018 Carabao Cup tie.

#1368. Michael Carrick facing the sack at Man United: Mauricio Pochettino the frontrunner to replace beleaguered boss - but chiefs face splashing out £7MILLION for former Spurs and Chelsea coach

Published: 18:04 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 02:44 EST, 10 November 2026

Michael Carrick is facing the sack with Manchester United bosses leaning towards installing a new head coach during the international break.

Carrick’s position has become increasingly precarious after United dropped into the relegation zone despite salvaging a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday.

It left the 45-year-old with just one win from 10 Premier League games this season – United’s worst start since Sir Alex Ferguson replaced Ron Atkinson 40 years ago.

Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as a new frontrunner to replace Carrick. The Argentine is currently in charge of the US national team, but his contract includes a £7million release clause.

Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann, who were both under consideration when United gave Carrick more time to turn the season around following a 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth last month, could also be in contention.

In the three games since then, Carrick’s side lost at Chelsea, staged a remarkable comeback to beat Roma in the Champions League in midweek and then fought back again to draw with Villa.

Michael Carrick is likely to be sacked from his role as Manchester United manager during the international break

It is understood that United officials have not made a final decision, though there is expectation that there will be a new boss in place after the international break

Although it’s understood that no final decision has been reached over Carrick’s future and insiders say that speculation over his sacking is premature, the expectation within Old Trafford is that a new man will be in charge for the visit to Anfield a week on Sunday.

Carrick replaced Ruben Amorim in mid-January and the former United midfielder was handed a two-year contract in May after guiding United to a third-place finish and qualification for the Champions League, losing just two of his 17 games as head coach.

But this season has unravelled alarmingly for United with his three wins in 15 games in all competitions coming at home to newly-promoted Ipswich in the Premier League as well as Sabah of Azerbaijan and Roma in the Champions League.

Asked after Sunday’s chaotic draw with Villa if he would consider quitting, a defiant Carrick said: ‘That's not going to happen.

‘We’re in November. I don’t like this situation and where we are. But we can do something about it. I'm quite clear with what direction the club needs to go in, and it's got to win games.’

Sacking Carrick would leave United searching for their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Ferguson retired 13-and-a-half years ago.

Pochettino was strongly linked with the job when Erik ten Hag was appointed in 2022 and again when the Dutchman was sacked two years later.

The 54-year-old has extensive Premier League experience at Tottenham, Chelsea and Southampton and was also in charge at Paris Saint-Germain.

Current US boss - and former Tottenham and Chelsea manager - Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as the frontrunner to replace Carrick

Howe was previously seen as the favourite but it’s understood there has been no contact between United and the former Newcastle boss.

It would cost United around £3million in compensation to appoint the 48-year-old under the terms of his departure from St James’s Park in July.

Nagelsmann is available after leaving his role as head coach of the German national team in the summer when they were eliminated from the World Cup following a penalty shootout defeat by Paraguay in the round of 32.

#1367. Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”

For all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage said. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

“It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really important to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”

With only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German said: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

You can also follow the latest updates from Manchester United’s crucial trip to Elland Road in our sister blog here.

#1365. Clearing the way for a transformative stem-cell treatment for Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Joohi Jimenez-Shahed studies movement disorders, neuromodulation and brain circuit therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Big improvements in Parkinson’s disease treatment have been few and far between. The tantalizing prospect of regenerative stem-cell therapies to address this neurodegenerative condition is therefore creating considerable excitement.

A core component of Parkinson’s is the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, which normally provide carefully controlled neurotransmitter signals to the brain’s movement circuits1. This leads to people having substantial difficulties performing routine activities.

A dopamine-replacement approach provided one of the first major advances in Parkinson’s treatment2. Levodopa, a chemical precursor to dopamine that was introduced in the 1960s, treats symptoms effectively. But the levodopa honeymoon can be short. As the effect duration of each dose wanes, extra doses or medications are required to keep dopamine levels from falling. And the drug can come with a complication that many patients dread — writhing, uncontrolled involuntary movements known as dyskinesia. A surgical approach called deep brain stimulation (DBS) can mitigate these complications effectively3.

The downsides of levodopa raise a question: rather than replacing dopamine, why not replace the cellular machinery that produces it? Enter the dopaminergic stem cell. Engineered from cells sampled from an adult’s own tissues (known as autologous) or from a different individual (allogeneic), induced-pluripotent stem cells can be safely transplanted into human brains and can improve movement-related Parkinson’s symptoms, such as tremors, stiffness and slowness, without worsening dyskinesia4.

Only a few dozen people have received this experimental treatment. Major brain surgery is required to transplant the cells. Allogeneic cell transplants also require recipients to undertake a year of immunosuppression to ensure that the cells survive. Autologous cell transplants avoid this, but it takes 6–8 months to produce the cells for each patient.

It is not yet known how cell therapies will measure up to current standards of care. Early studies have been in people with advanced disease. At this stage, the chance of benefit might be reduced: the cells are implanted into an already degenerating circuit that could be difficult to restore.

Critics might therefore argue that dopamine cell therapies cannot produce a more robust effect than levodopa or DBS without imposing excess cost or risk. But the way that Parkinson’s treatments are investigated and approved can neither fully support this pessimistic view nor provide sufficient evidence for a more optimistic one.

Therapeutic development for Parkinson’s has mainly aimed to relieve symptoms. A more ambitious goal would be to slow the disease’s progression by altering its underlying biology. Yet there are substantial obstacles to developing such a treatment.

Implicit to the concept of disease modification is the need for a biomarker that measures the underlying biological processes5. Although a biological definition of Parkinson’s is emerging, it applies mainly to the identification of early disease. Relatively little is known about how such markers evolve in Parkinson’s, or how they relate to clinical progression6.

Long-term, multi-site observational studies such as the Parkinson’s Precision Medicine Initiative (see go.nature.com/4ayapbI) provide an ideal framework for exploring digital, biological and imaging markers, while benchmarking disease progression. Their success depends on building and sustaining large consortia, and on a healthy dose of time and effort from researchers and study participants, but the studies are constrained by funding inequities.

Even if such biomarkers were already at researchers’ disposal, there is no specific guidance from the US Food and Drug Administration on developing disease-modifying treatments7. The agency’s Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy designation speeds up cell- and gene-therapy development and approval. But eligibility requires only the intent to treat, modify, reverse or cure a serious disorder. As a result, clinical trials of regenerative therapies are likely to be designed to show benefits to a person’s symptoms without incurring the added cost and burden of showing a change in biology — a pragmatic but less ambitious path.

Crucially, supportive evidence for the broader potential of dopaminergic cell therapies is what will define their advantage. Cell dose, optimal treatment timing and objective evidence of cell survival, engraftment and effects on brain-network function would demonstrate whether cell therapies can produce lasting change in people with Parkinson’s. Public–private research partnerships could refine the required measurement tools and generate such data.

The ability to transform stem cells into dopamine-producing neurons and transplant them safely into human brains is momentous. Its use as a treatment extends an opportunity to chart another course for people with Parkinson’s by limiting levodopa complications and possibly the need for DBS. This outcome would bolster the hopes of people with this condition. But the real therapeutic breakthrough will occur only when scientists and regulators converge to advance the goal of restoring neural circuitry and function. That would be a truly bold step towards conquering this this relentless disease.
