#1308. Sensational Spurs storm Stamford Bridge as Palmer loses his head

So much for Xabi Alonso’s call for cool heads from his Chelsea players. Cole Palmer lost his and was sent off, while goalkeeper Mike Penders punched the ball into his own net to give Tottenham Hotspur a helping hand on their way to a second win at Stamford Bridge in 42 attempts.

This was hardly “the Battle of the Bridge”, but Chelsea blew up during a ridiculous 10-minute spell towards the end of a game in which Tottenham had bossed possession but not looked like scoring.

Palmer was lucky to stay on the pitch in the 70th minute, when he shoved his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes after the Tottenham midfielder had stopped him racing through with a foul and a handball.

Christopher Kavanagh, the referee, let him off with a yellow card, but 10 minutes later Palmer inexplicably gave Kavanagh no choice but to book him again and send him off, following a late challenge on substitute Conor Gallagher.

"It's PETULANT from Cole Palmer...you have to take it on the chin" Jamie Redknapp and Daniel Sturridge react to Cole Palmer's pair of yellow cards 🟥 https://t.co/Voxoo3Ea7V

Palmer was just about the only Chelsea player not to have been sent off last season, but it seems that Alonso has not yet managed to deal with the club’s disciplinary problem.

Jordan Henderson had given Palmer a talking to at the end of the win at Everton in which the forward was booked. But he evidently did not heed the advice or the words of his manager.

Alonso had said he was confident his players could keep calm ahead of the game, but he got that wrong – along with his team selection and substitutions.

In between Palmer’s two bookings, Penders suffered his own moment of madness with a bizarre own goal on his league debut for Chelsea. The Belgian was standing in for Emi Martinez, who watched in disbelief from the home dug-out after undergoing surgery on his jaw.

Fernandes sent in a corner that Jan Paul van Hecke challenged for. Penders looked like the easy winner in that contest, but he got his punch horribly wrong and the ball spun backwards and over the goalline.

Spurs have taken the lead after Mateus Fernandes' corner ends up in Chelsea's goal ⚽️ https://t.co/X65gyO9yPX

A man and a goal down, Chelsea then saw hundreds of their own fans walk out when Mathys Tel scored a brilliant second for Spurs with three minutes remaining. The visiting fans, who had seen one win at the Bridge since 1990 prior to Saturday, could hardly believe what they had seen.

"Just look what it means!" A glorious solo run and finish from Mathys Tel! 🤩 https://t.co/Qg7WMFNlwQ

Tottenham head coach Roberto De Zerbi celebrated wildly with his staff. The two benches had clashed and De Zerbi had been booked after Palmer’s first yellow card that the Italian felt should have been a red. But De Zerbi will not care about that now, with Tottenham’s season finally up and running thanks to successive league wins against Coventry City and Chelsea.

"They were brilliant Spurs, they really were" Gary Neville's immediate reaction to Chelsea 0-2 Tottenham 🗣️ https://t.co/QWhi7Blmfz

Tottenham should really have been ahead in the first half. De Zerbi revealed before the game that Dominic Solanke had dropped down to the substitutes’ bench because the striker “felt fatigue” after the victory over Coventry.

With Solanke resting up on the bench until the 65th minute, De Zerbi moved Omar Marmoush, who had scored his first Spurs goal against Coventry, into the middle and brought in Tel on the left.

Tel was involved in the 29th-minute move that should have resulted in the opening goal for Marmoush. The Frenchman played a one-two with Andy Robertson and the Scotsman picked out Marmoush with a low cross. But, six yards out and with time to pick his spot, the former Manchester City man allowed Penders to make a save.

The missed Marmoush chance was the first time Penders had been called into action. At the other end, Tottenham goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky made unnecessary work for himself.

Kinsky played a bad pass straight to Pedro Neto. The ball was worked to Henderson, but Kinsky recovered to make a save and then stopped the follow-up from Neto. The offside flag then went up, but it was unclear whether it would have spared Kinsky on both occasions had Chelsea scored.

It was not the first time Kinsky had handed possession back to Chelsea in a dangerous area, although the 23-year-old had also made a good save to palm away a curling effort from Palmer. That came after Fernandes had the ball pinched from him far too easily.

Neto was Chelsea’s most dangerous player, but it was the wrong call by Alonso to leave Danny Welbeck on the bench, with João Pedro out injured, and he was too slow to change things. Leaving it until the 88th minute, when the game had already been killed by Tel, to send on the striker was a clear error.

Storm Boelo created wet-and-wild conditions on the Stamford Bridge pitch, while there were still remnants of Storm Austen, or should that be Storm Austin, on the home bench.

Chelsea set-piece coach Austin MacPhee let out an incredibly loud “for f---’s sake” when one corner routine went wrong. Nobody could hear what he was shouting over the Tottenham celebrations when Penders scored his own goal, but it would almost certainly have started with “f” again.

James Maddison had been a doubt before the game after missing training during the week and it only took four minutes of the second half for him to signal to De Zerbi that he needed to come off.

Maddison had scored a brilliant goal on his first league start in 18 months against Coventry, but he had to be replaced by former Chelsea midfielder Gallagher at Stamford Bridge.

James Maddison is forced off with an injury and is replaced by Conor Gallagher, who receives a mixed reception from his former fans 🔃 https://t.co/GSeXQQ3eoa

The Chelsea fans predictably booed Gallagher, a graduate of the club’s academy who at times even stood in as captain. The foul on Gallagher that earned Palmer his marching orders silenced the jeers and the Chelsea fans’ boos only returned at the final whistle for their own players.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has told Cole Palmer he must learn from his red card that contributed to his team’s London derby defeat by Tottenham Hotspur.

Tottenham head coach Roberto De Zerbi insisted Palmer should have seen red for shoving his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes. But, having got off with a yellow card, the Chelsea midfielder then fouled substitute Conor Gallagher.

“I haven’t seen them [the yellow cards] on TV, but as far as I have been told, he [the referee] probably got it right,” Alonso said. “So, for sure for Cole, but for everyone. We think [up until] now we haven’t received any red cards [this season] and we need to continue that way because we need to have this maturity to deal with difficult moments, when you have conceded 1-0, there was still 15-20 minutes to go, so we have to be calm. I need to check the action to talk with Cole, but it is one to learn for the future for sure.”

Asked if he thought Palmer should have been sent off for the first yellow card, De Zerbi, who was booked for his protests, replied: “Yep.”

Jordan Henderson had spoken to Palmer at the end of the previous week’s victory over Everton in which the forward could also have been booked for a second time and sent off.

But Alonso claimed he does not have any wider concerns about Palmer’s character. He said: “Today, for sure, yes, but it is not a [wider] concern. I think that Cole when he is focused on the game, when he is enjoying and today after the 1-0, it is a moment to keep calm, a moment to keep mature and for everyone.”

De Zerbi hailed his side’s character and claimed that Tottenham have “suffered enough” after two 17th-placed finishes and a slow start to the season until successive victories over Coventry City and Chelsea.

“We want to improve, improve and improve, to be better game by game, week by week. I think we have suffered enough,” De Zerbi said. “Changing the spirit of the group, changing the performance of the players, especially the more fragile players, maybe the younger players. We played very well. Great individual performances, great collective performance because we played very well. And then we put something different than Tottenham, I think, in the last period. Different attitude, different relationships with the players, different group.”

Chelsea were without João Pedro because of an injury and Alonso is waiting to find out how long the striker will be out.

“We don’t know yet because he has a lot of fluid,” Alonso said. “So he felt it yesterday [Friday] and we need to wait probably until tomorrow [Sunday] to do the test and to know the whole situation and the whole seriousness of the injury. We will know soon enough.”

A long-awaited Stamford Bridge victory for @SpursOfficial 👏 https://t.co/Qqwgbuj3Y3

“When we have dinner together and spend time together in the dressing room, I see a different group, different relationships and a different atmosphere among the players.

“The character was great today, but we have many, many new players. The players who stayed here from last season and two or three seasons ago suffered from the results, including two 17th-place finishes.

“We are working to change the last part of the club’s history. We are lucky because we have many great people in the dressing room and many great players. I think if we work hard, we can do something important.

“The week in Marbella, speaking face to face, opening ourselves up and removing the mask, was important for the spirit and belief.

“The atmosphere inside the dressing room is maybe more important than the tactics.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Tottenham boss said: “It was a big moment for the fans, the club and the players. They deserved this win and prepared very well.

“We are improving a lot in our mentality, as a group and in our relationships with the players. We are also improving on the pitch.

“Against Aston Villa and Everton, for 30 minutes we were playing very well. Maybe we didn’t score because our finishing wasn’t good enough, and perhaps in the first difficult moment we changed our mentality.

“Now we are a complete team. The players are playing better and we have improved our style.

“I have to believe in this group. I never lost confidence in my players.

“We have to keep working hard and improving. We have many great players, and I believe we can do something important if we continue in this way.”

It’s half-time at Stamford Bridge in a game lacking chances and attacking threat. Tottenham came closest to scoring just before the half-hour mark, when Marmoush forced Penders into terrific save on his first Premier League start. At the other end, Palmers tested Kinsky with a whipped effort, which the Spurs goalkeeper parried away. There’s much to ponder for Chelsea boss Alonso, whose plan to start to without a recognised striker has underwhelmed, while De Zerbi will feel more encouraged by his side’s display.

Hato takes a quick, clever free kick and finds Pedro Neto, whose made a great run. The winger flashes a low, driven shot off the wet surface from a tight angle, but Kinsky is there to gather it.

Spurs come forward on the counter through Tel, Marmoush and Kudus. However, the attack seems to lack conviction and it ends with Mateus Fernandes’ arrowed cross harmlessly drifting out of play.

We’re still waiting for this game to explode into life. It’s lacked the normal drama and controversy that this fixture normally provides.

Chelsea come alive as Kinsky miscues his pass, giving the ball to Pedro Neto. Spurs burst forward on the counter and threads a pass through to Tel. Penders rushes out to smother the winger’s one-on-one effort. The offside flag was up, but Penders still did well to make the intervention.

Massive chance for Tottenham. Robertson slides a low, pinpoint cross into Marmoush, who shoots first-time from close range. Penders is up to the challenge and makes a pivotal stop to parry it away.

Penders comes out of his box and unconvincingly intercepts a through ball over the top of Chelsea’s defence. His pass has no power, but luckily for the young goalkeeper, it lands at Lacroix’s feet.

Spurs aren’t playing with their usual inferiority complex at Stamford Bridge. They looking confident. Chelsea are yet to strike a rhythm. Tel darts into Chelsea’s box, but Pedro Neto tracks back and makes an important tackle.

Chelsea’s substitutes have just been handed fluffy white towels to keep themselves dry and warm. I want one.

Tel’s deep cross finds Kudus at the back stick. The Ghanaian bends a curling strike around the covering defender. However, the shot evades the far post. Tottenham can certainly be encouraged by their start to this game.

Lacroix denies Maddison with a brilliant sliding challenge to win a goal kick for Chelsea. Maddison was convinced it was a corner.

We just heard a rather loud “For f***s sake” from Chelsea set-piece coach Austin MacPhee. Given we’ve just had Storm Austen, it feels appropriate that the Scotsman is giving the players a battering.

Pedro Neto does excellently to dispossess Mateus Fernandes, allowing Rogers to tee up Palmer. The playmaker whips a fierce effort aimed for the far top corner, but Kinsky is there to make a eye-catching diving save.

Tottenham have had more of the early possession, but both teams are still sounding each other out as we await the game’s first big chance. Palmers, Rogers and Henderson attempt a cheeky free kick routine, but Kinsky is alert to the danger.

Kinsky comes out of his box and Chelsea pounce on his poor pass to launch an attack. Palmer fizzes a delightful cross into the box, but no one is there to get on the end of it. Where’s Joao Pedro when you need him?

Rogers is playing highest for Chelsea as a false striker. He did it a few times for Villa, so it shouldn’t be anything new to him.

An early spell of Tottenham sees Chelsea defend a couple of free-kicks and clear a corner.

There will be no out-and-out strikers on the pitch today. Joao Pedro is out for Chelsea with an, as yet unspecified injury, while De Zerbi has said that Dominic Solanke “felt fatigue” against Coventry City so he has dropped to the bench. Antonio Conte, a former manager of both of these teams, wouldn’t be having a player missing a London derby for “feeling fatigue”.

Chelsea get us under way. The rain is hammering down on the pitch.

#1307. Liberali reveals first thing Fabregas told him after Como switch and Italy idol

Como talent Mattia Liberali reveals the first thing Cesc Fabregas told him this summer, names Francesco Totti as one of his Italy idols and jokes about Alphadjo Cisse: ‘If you text him, he replies after three days.’

Liberali held a press conference at Coverciano on Tuesday, joining his former Catanzaro teammate Cisse.

Both have received their first senior Italy call-up for the November break.

Liberali was asked about the merits and defects of Cisse, and he replied smiling: “Starting with the defects: if you text him, he replies three days later. He lives in his own world, but that’s also one of his strengths because, on the pitch, he knows how to shut everything out and always plays with a carefree mindset, as we’ve seen in recent months,” he said.

“In the matches where I started playing last season [at Catanzaro], we played together. It was a great year, but it was also difficult at the beginning. You have to make the most of those moments and use them to work on yourself in training. The rewards have come, and we need to keep going like this. It’s only the beginning.”

Liberali scored three goals and provided four assists in 24 Serie B appearances with Catanzaro last season, but he wasn’t initially a regular starter under Alberto Aquilani, and the way he handled the situation impressed his current Como coach, Fàbregas.

“The first thing he told me on day one was congratulations on these last two years,” Liberali said.

“He liked how I stayed focused even when I wasn’t playing in the first few months, and he appreciated the choices I made.

“Fàbregas is a great coach. In just a few years, he has taken Como to the point of fighting for Champions League places and the league title. He’s helping me a lot, giving me a lot of confidence, and so far things are going really well. The group is young, just like here with the national team. They’re all great guys; they work hard, and the atmosphere is very positive.

“For a young player, Como’s environment is excellent and very important,” Liberali added.

“Being young doesn’t automatically mean you’ll play. You have to earn your opportunities and be ready when they come. It’s an ambitious club and an ambitious environment.

“I didn’t expect the [Como] group to be this united. I think that makes a huge difference. Fighting for one another means a lot in international football and in the Champions League. What really matters is the team’s unity, and in these matches we’ve shown that at our best.”

Liberali also sent a message to his ex-coach, Aquilani, who Sassuolo sacked on Monday.

“I’m sorry about Aquilani. I’ll text him in the next few days. I owe him a lot. Last year he gave me so much, both as a coach and on a personal level,” he said.

How does it feel to receive his first Italy call-up?

“I didn’t expect it, but it has had a big impact on me,” Liberali said.

“It’s an honor to be here. Both in football and beyond, there are important people around. They welcomed us like family from day one, and we’re settling in very well.

“It’s not easy to go from Serie B to Serie A and the Champions League in terms of intensity, but with hard work you can adapt if you are focused and know what you want.

“In today’s football, you need technical quality, but you also have to be physically prepared. The intensity is very high, and you have to be ready. There are many outstanding players here, like Vergara and Pisilli. It’s important to have players of that caliber.”

Has he received any specific request from Italy coach Roberto Mancini?

“He didn’t ask anything extraordinary of me, just to stay calm and train the way I know how. Everyone welcomed me warmly. The key is to stay relaxed and keep training as always.

[U21] coach Baldini helped me a lot, even though I only spent two weeks in preseason training with him. He’s very experienced, but before he became a coach, he focused on helping young players grow as people.

“A carefree mindset is the foundation for stepping onto the pitch. In the end, football is a game. You shouldn’t put extra pressure on yourself because plenty already comes from outside. Right now, we have everything to gain and nothing to lose.”

Liberali refused to return to Milan, opting instead to move to Como. Does he have any regret seeing how quickly Cisse has adapted?

“No regrets. As I often say, make decisions with conviction and without looking back,” Liberali said.

“Leaving Milan wasn’t easy, but I’m very happy for Alpha. I text him often. But no, I have no regrets. It’s right to look forward, not backward.”

“There’s not much to say about France,” Liberali argued.

“They have undeniable world-class talent. We believe in qualification, and we’ll give absolutely everything we have.”

Lastly, Liberali named one of his Azzurri role models.

“There are plenty of role models to choose from, and many great players. Even the coach himself is a fantastic example. I’ve always liked Totti,” he concluded.

Lorenzo Bettoni is the Editor of Football Italia.

#1306. Mauricio Pochettino Appointment Can Save Lisandro Martinez's Man Utd Career

Manchester United are in a crisis, and the board look set to make the decision that a change is necessary.

United sit 18th in the Premier League with just one win in 10 Premier League games so far this season, while they have won just 3 of 14 in all competitions under Carrick, and GIVEMESPORT sources understand that the iconic former midfielder is set to be relieved of his duties at Old Trafford as a result.

Speculation has been rife for several weeks about his future, and who could potentially replace him, and it has now emerged that USMNT boss Mauricio Pochettino is currently a leading candidate for the role.

The Argentine has got plenty of Premier League and Champions League experience, having managed Southampton, Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain, and Chelsea before taking up his role as boss of the United States, where he led the team to the Last 16 at the 2026 World Cup, before being rewarded with a new four-year deal.

But that contract is understood to have a $10m (£7.4m) release clause, which could open the door for him to return to England once again, and finally get the Man Utd job he has been pining for since 2019.

His arrival would be a mark of intent from INEOS, and potentially a final roll of the dice for board members like Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada, who have so far failed to live up to their reputation of being 'best in class' since being brought in.

However, on the pitch, his appointment could also be a saving grace for some players or a dagger in the heart for others, who may not fit in with his style of play or how he sees football.

One player who could potentially be handed a reprieve at Old Trafford under the 54-year-old is his fellow countryman, Lisandro Martinez, who has been strongly linked with an exit away from the club in 2027.

The central defender has been in terrible form in recent weeks, having been at fault for a number of goals, before a ridiculous red card against Chelsea led to the team's collapse in a 3-0 defeat at Stamford Bridge. But more than that was his public outburst against the club hierarchy, where he admitted to feeling let down by the summer business and the strength of the squad. He has been labelled as being part of a 'toxic' culture at the club by pundit Adam Joseph.

Martinez is out of contract at Man Utd at the end of the season, and while the club have the option to extend by a further 12 months, reports have suggested they will not be looking to trigger that.

But with Pochettino being a manager who likes to dominate possession and build up from the back, the quality that Martinez has and his leadership qualities will likely be huge for the coach when it comes to implementing his style in the short-term.

Martinez had been a firm fan favourite until this season, and should he be able to string together a run of top performances and United start to turn the season around, he would likely be back in the good books quickly. That could force INEOS' hand when it comes to his contract situation, and could also convince the player that he is at the right club after all.

With funds understood to be limited, finding a replacement immediately for Martinez will be difficult. Pochettino won't want to be handicapped anymore if he is stepping in mid-season, and that could be the perfect remedy for a reprieve.

#1305. Hearts boss Vrancken is playing with fire by turning the guns on his own players

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:17 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 12:26 EST, 10 November 2026

Not for the first time this season under Wouter Vrancken, Hearts suffered a complete and utter implosion as they were thrashed 5-2 at home to Falkirk last weekend.

This is a team who lost 6-0 to Sturm Graz over two legs in the Champions League qualifiers back at the start of the campaign.

A team who were then battered 6-1 away against Benfica in Lisbon in the Europa League qualifiers – and a team who were also thumped 7-1 against Celtic at Parkhead a few weeks ago.

Hearts also lost the derby to Hibs just over a week ago in the semi-finals of the Premier Sports Cup at Hampden.

Now comes an annihilation against Falkirk where Hearts were 4-0 down by half-time. What a shambolic way to lose a long unbeaten record at home.

Even accounting for what had gone before in some of those matches this season, what happened on Sunday at Tynecastle felt like a new low.

Hearts were a shambles. But what was even more alarming was the manager's inability to stop the bleeding and make any changes from the touchline.

All of which poses a very simple question. Have Hearts and Jamestown made a mistake with Vrancken? At the moment, he looks hopelessly one-dimensional.

But it was his post-match comments on Sunday afternoon which actually became even more alarming than the performance itself.

Wouter Vrancken was 'embarrassed' by Hearts' 5-2 home loss to Falkirk

Vrancken branded it 'embarrassing' and a 'disgrace'. He called his players 'childish' and basically insinuated that they lacked any spirit or character until the youngsters came off the bench.

In the midst of a horrendous injury crisis and with players dropping like flies, that is a very dangerous game for any manager to play. He threw them under a bus.

By publicly slaughtering his players like that during a time of adversity and when many of them are being asked to play out of position, he is playing with fire.

Those are the type of comments that could very easily lose a dressing room. His comments would have gone down like a lead balloon among the squad.

Hearts have had the best part of a dozen players missing through injury. Vrancken himself has branded it an injury crisis unlike any other he has experienced throughout his career.

But what is most curious in all of this is that Vrancken seems totally unwilling to engage in any self-reflection throughout all of this.

After the shellacking at Celtic Park a few weeks ago, he lamented the fact his team had made too many individual errors.

There was no acknowledgment that his system had set them up to fail. No acceptance that pressing Celtic man-for-man and leaving players one-v-one at the back was a huge part of the problem.

Since he arrived in the summer, Vrancken's preferred style of play has been front-foot attacking football. There have been times when it has clicked reasonably well.

When he had his key players fit, Hearts were a good watch. But when the guts of a full team were then ripped out due to injury, it has quickly disintegrated into chaos.

Continuing to demand the same high-pressing and attacking style of play without meaningful adjustment is not principled. It is naive, inflexible, and tactically illiterate.

When the structure collapses, as it did against Falkirk and in the 7-1 defeat at Celtic, the emphasis returns to individual mistakes rather than collective vulnerability created by the system itself.

It is a classic example of a manager publicly hanging his players out to dry rather than choosing to accept his own part in the wider failings.

Hearts are not in crisis yet. They still sit fourth in the table, just a point behind Falkirk. But this is a team who have clearly regressed from where they were last season.

Vrancken was hired on the basis that he could bring a more dynamic style of play and move the team forward from the platform left behind by Derek McInnes.

As written in these pages a few weeks ago after the defeat to Celtic, there is absolutely no prospect whatsoever of this Hearts team challenging for the title this time around.

The current combination of a horrendous injury list, a rigid tactical approach and increasingly pointed public criticism of the players is a dangerous mixture that threatens to undermine everything.

Scottish football's fixture congestion, the demands of European competition and the physical toll of the season have exposed the limits of Vrancken's one-dimensional plan.

Adaptation is not a betrayal of principles. It is a basic requirement of the job when circumstances change this dramatically.

The international break offers a brief window. A handful of bodies may return for Hearts' next fixture against Dundee at Dens Park.

The more important return would be a change in tone and a willingness to adapt the demands placed on those players left still standing.

Publicly branding his players as 'a disgrace' while refusing to acknowledge that the system itself is contributing to their vulnerability is a sure-fire way to get himself sacked.

Vrancken's Hearts squad has been ravaged by injuries this season

The manager is entitled to be angry. He is entitled to demand better. He is not entitled to ignore the context he is operating in or the effect his words will have on a group already stretched to breaking point.

Vrancken arrived with a clear identity and early promise. The test now is whether he can evolve that identity under pressure or whether he remains locked into one way of playing regardless of the resources available.

Hearts cannot afford the latter. Much more of this public slaughtering and the players will switch off. Vrancken will have lost them completely.

Players will run for a manager who shows understanding of their situation even while criticising their standards.

They will begin to switch off for one who appears to place the preservation of his methods above the protection of the group.

That is the risk Vrancken is running. It is a risk no manager in the middle of a crippling injury crisis can afford to take.

#1304. Inter’s Thuram renewal talks off to a slow start as Oaktree wage policy bites

Inter have started talks over a new contract for Marcus Thuram, but the negotiations have got off to a difficult start.

According to Tuttosport, the Nerazzurri want to extend the French striker’s deal, which runs until 2028, by another three years. Thuram currently earns €6.5m a season plus bonuses that can take him close to €8m, making him one of the best-paid players in the squad.

Under Oaktree’s new policy, Inter want to cut the wages of players in their thirties. Beppe Marotta and Dario Baccin are therefore offering a fixed salary of €4.5-5m, with bonuses and benefits that would take it back up to his current €6.5m.

Thuram isn’t keen on that structure, especially as he doesn’t turn 30 until August. Foreign clubs are also monitoring the situation ahead of next summer. The forward wants to prioritise Inter, but he’s pushing to keep at least his current terms.

He’s become even more important to Cristian Chivu’s side since Lautaro Martínez got injured, with four goals and two assists in six league games. Inter’s only Serie A defeat so far, in the derby, was the one game in that run in which Thuram didn’t score or assist.

#1303. Man Utd Hold Discussions Over 'Exceptional' Nagelsmann Instead of Pochettino

Manchester United have also held internal discussions over the appointment of Julian Nagelsmann amid links with UMSNT boss Mauricio Pochettino. The Red Devils are expected to sack Michael Carrick after a torrid start to the season that has seen United win just one of their first 10 Premier League games.

Carrick did oversee a comeback win over AS Roma in the Champions League and a comeback draw with Aston Villa in the Premier League over the weekend, but those results do not look to be sufficient to have saved the former midfielder.

The sacking decision hasn't been made yet, but with reports gathering pace, attention is already turning to who could be next in at Old Trafford. USMNT boss Pochettino is one of the main candidates, available for $10million due to a release clause in his US Soccer contract.

But that is an expensive bill to pay for a manager, and United have other irons in the fire, namely former Germany boss Nagelsmann, who has previously won a league and cup double with Bayern Munich, while he also impressed with RB Leipzig, though his spell with Germany ended in disappointment.

GIVEMESPORT's Ben Jacobs has posted on X: "Michael Carrick's #MUFC contract contains a break clause, making an exit more affordable than with previous Manchester United managers. Mauricio Pochettino, one of the leading contenders for the role, also has a release clause, which multiple sources believe will not prove prohibitive if #MUFC choose to proceed. The former Spurs and Chelsea boss is open to the role despite only recently extended his contract with US Soccer.

"Free agents Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann have also been discussed. £3m due to Newcastle if Howe was to be appointed."

Pochettino will be the most attractive option, while Howe has already split opinion among United fans, who may feel as though the appointment would not be ambitious enough. Howe has worked his way up the Premier League at AFC Bournemouth and Newcastle United, but he does not have any experience at a top club, and United need to finally appoint a manager with top-level experience.

As for Nagelsmann, he has spent time at the top of the game, but one could argue that his results have not been of an elite level.

It's never easy to win a league or a cup, but at Bayern Munich, it's an easier task, and he struggled with a very talented Germany side.

Still, at 39 years of age, Nagelsmann has an impressive CV, and you would like to think he will only continue to improve having already worked with plenty of elite players.

Current Germany boss Jurgen Klopp, who replaced Nagelsmann, has previously said of his predecessor:

“Julian coached a Bundesliga team in Germany when he was 28, which is a really exceptional story.”

“Being at that age, now he is in the age I was when I started coaching but he is doing it already for five or six years, which is really exceptional. Still young. “I'm afraid to say, but probably will still get better and better over the years, like we all got, but is already really highest quality.”

That's a verdict to take notice of, with Klopp knowing very well what makes a top coach, and the added benefit of Nagelsmann is that he would arrive at Old Trafford for free and save the Red Devils around £7.5million.

#1302. Parkinson’s: beyond the brain

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Parkinson’s research has focused mostly on the brain, and the processes that lead to the death of dopamine neurons, which eventually causes the varied symptoms of the neurodegenerative disease. But given that research has not uncovered a genetic component for most people, what triggers the disease has remained elusive. Some researchers have begun to investigate how environmental factors — including exposure to herbicides, pesticides and air pollution — could be an important factor in the increasing number of cases. Others, meanwhile, have found that the clumping of proteins that drives the disease might begin in the gut rather than in the brain.

This film investigates these avenues of research, and shares what it could mean in preventing and treating the disease.

#1301. Most expensive goal in Liverpool history gives Iraola era lift-off

A quick sprint, a well-placed pass and an instinctive finish. Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak will have done this dozens of times in training but here, on a squally Sunday afternoon, this combination secured a little piece of history.

Anfield has witnessed plenty of significant goals down the years but never had this crowd seen one that cost £248m to make. Liverpool invested a near quarter-billion pounds on Barcola and Isak for bigger occasions than a tussle with Brighton and Hove Albion, but this rapid interchange felt like a significant moment.

Liverpool are a work in progress under Andoni Iraola but with each minute of each game you can see signs of things knitting together, and if Barcola and Isak are finding harmony, with Florian Wirtz in behind, then, perhaps, this journey will start to accelerate.

This was an important afternoon for Liverpool’s head coach, a difficult assignment against high-flying, well-respected opponents in Brighton, who arrived on Merseyside having won their last four Premier League fixtures with a combined aggregate of 15-0, including a 3-0 thumping of reigning champions Arsenal.

But Liverpool rose impressively to the challenge and there are grounds for saying this was the most significant success to date for Iraola, whose team defended relentlessly to preserve a clean sheet. They are up to fourth now after this 2-0 success and deserve their position.

“I’m very happy,” Iraola said. “We faced a very good opponent, similar to Villarreal [in the Champions League]. It’s difficult to defend them a lot of times and it was key how we started. We needed to be aggressive, recover balls, win our duels, be dangerous in transitions: I think we’ve done it.”

And how. Iraola was able to march towards the Kop at the end, to clap the supporters and acknowledge only Liverpool’s fifth (and his first) Premier League win at Anfield in 2026, and it was evident he had a spring in his step from what he had seen.

Whether the game would have flowed in the direction it did had Brighton taken the lead can only be speculated but what a glorious chance they wasted for us to find out: in the 13th minute, five swift, one-touch passes bamboozled Liverpool’s defence and created space for Yasin Ayari.

With the goal at his mercy, Ayari could have made things exceptionally uncomfortable but he leant back and blazed over. He clasped his face and grimaced, knowing what had gone begging in front of the Kop; four minutes later, his misery was exacerbated.

"He's GOT to hit the target!" Yasin Ayari missed a golden chance to put Brighton ahead against Liverpool 🫣 https://t.co/Qz7G3sXCpP

Liverpool’s lead was secured with an element of good fortune but, equally, the tenacity of Ronald Araújo and Wirtz was instrumental in pressing Brighton back to the point that they were panicking; Wirtz’s shot, deflected off Pascal Gross past Bart Verbruggen, compounded it all.

“I think everyone in the stadium – and you as well – felt there was a missed opportunity for us,” groaned Fabian Hürzeler, the visitors’ head coach. “It’s not only after the goal or the goals they scored. Before they scored, we had two big chances. I think it was just the difference that they scored and we didn’t score.”

It would be wrong to say Wirtz was doing cartwheels – perhaps he knew immediately he would not get the goal – but it was an important moment for him and you could feel the sense of goodwill towards him from team-mates and supporters alike.

Florian Wirtz's deflected shot has put Liverpool ahead minutes after Brighton had a great chance of their own ⚽️ https://t.co/b6mRvl2rSR

Remarkably, this was the first time Liverpool had scored in the first half at Anfield in a Premier League fixture since May 9 and, with that momentum, it led to one of those periods when they started attacking in waves and carried the crowd with them.

What they needed was a second goal to arrive quite quickly and that is what happened when Barcola won possession, scuttled forward and played a perfectly weighted bobbling ball into Isak’s path; the Swede did the rest, calmly finishing from eight yards.

#1300. Man Utd Make Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada Sack Decision

Manchester United are believed to have already reached their verdict not just on the future of Michael Carrick, but also regarding two other key higher-ups, Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox, who have also received serious scrutiny over recent months.

With multiple outlets now reporting that the former Man Utd midfielder turned interim boss and now full-time head coach is set to be relieved of his duties in the very near future – and with United's preferred candidate to replace Michael Carrick already named – pundits, supporters, and football fans in general are debating where exactly the book stops at the giant of a sporting brand, as countless have questioned where the true accountability for their poor fortunes in the post-Fergie era lies.

Berrada and Wilcox, both of whom found success on the business side of things during their time at Man City, are now the latest to be targeted by chants around Old Trafford and protest banners hanging from stands in the Stretford End.

Manchester United chiefs are expected to sack Michael Carrick

Nevertheless, while they're still trying to back their manager and thank him for his efforts during one of the most difficult periods in the club's long history, GIVEMESPORT understands that the pair are safe. At least for now, anyway.

As per The Telegraph's James Ducker and other sources, the executive duo — Berrada serving as CEO and Wilcox as Director of Football, respectively — are expected to keep their jobs if/when Carrick is dismissed; it's said they maintain co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe's support as part of a core triumvirate.

Since INEOS' investment in Manchester United, they have already shuffled significantly not only when it comes to the backroom staff but within the boardroom too, but it looks as though he still considers them key advisers and pillars of the so-called 'Project 2028' rebuild.

Ratcliffe has reiterated that, despite stating that he doesn't mind being "unpopular" and making the tough decisions, the increasing levels of abuse he and his cohort have received over the course of their tenure at the club, stating that he would walk away from the whole franchise if it ever became severe and prolonged as the anti-ownership sentiment and demonstrations the Glazer family have seen.

On the one hand, Wilcox's involvement in footballing decisions has been perceived as an issue by many Reds (this being the ex-player's first role of this kind), with divisive defender Lisandro Martínez publicly criticising the sporting director's decision-making in his highly inflammatory post-match quotes following their Champions League defeat to Atlético Madrid.

Meanwhile, more senior 'leadership' figures such as the World Cup winner himself have equally come under fire for sub-par performances of late, making key match-deciding errors and, crucially, irrespective of whatever big statements made in high-profile interviews, not doing enough talking on the pitch.

For most United match-goers and fans who watch it with their eyes week in, week out, whether or not Carrick stays or goes won't be enough to fix the deep-seated problems running throughout Manchester United; they'd much prefer wholesale change from the very top of the hierarchy all the way down - though it's likely they'll be waiting a long time to see that on a big enough scale to quell their frustrations.

'Green gold until the club is sold', as the supporters' saying goes, but do any of you really foresee the Glazers selling up one of the biggest sporting franchises in the world anytime soon?

#1299. De Gea’s Fiorentina tenure nearly over as Viola prepare to move on from ex-Man Utd goalkeeper

David De Gea’s time at Fiorentina could be coming to an end, with the Viola already looking at possible replacements for the former Manchester United goalkeeper.

According to Corriere dello Sport, the club have growing doubts about the 36-year-old because of his errors this season and his €3.5m net-a-year salary.

Paolo Vanoli defended his captain after Sunday’s 2-2 draw with Juventus, insisting De Gea isn’t a problem. Even so, the Spaniard was at fault for Gleison Bremer’s goal in the 66th minute, when he started to come off his line for a cross and then stayed put. He has also made mistakes against Sassuolo, Como, Genoa, Frosinone and Roma, and coming for crosses, long a weakness, appears to have got worse with age.

The current back-ups, Oliver Christensen and Luca Lezzerini, aren’t seen as long-term solutions, and sporting director Fabio Paratici has started to look elsewhere.

Tommaso Martinelli is the first option. The Fiorentina-owned goalkeeper is currently on loan at Serie B side Avellino. The club are also exploring the international market, and River Plate’s Santiago Beltrán, born in 2004, is among the names being linked.

The Corriere believes these could be De Gea’s final seven months in Florence.

#1298. Pochettino Would Make Marcus Rashford His Next Son Heung-Min Son at Man Utd

Manchester United are planning for life after Michael Carrick, and Mauricio Pochettino is the man they are looking to make their next manager.

The Red Devils have won just three of their 14 games in all competitions, including just one of their 10 Premier League games, leaving them 18th in the table heading into the November international break - their worst ever start to a Premier League season.

That form is set to see Carrick sacked, with GIVEMESPORT sources understanding that Sir Jim Ratcliffe will head a meeting in Monaco in Wednesday where his future will be confirmed one way or another. Former Spurs boss Pochettino is considered to be a leading target to replace him, with the USA boss having a $10m (£7.4m) release clause in his contract that would make him available immediately.

During his time in north London, Pochettino rebuilt the squad and saw them reach an EFL Cup and Champions League final, while they also finished second in the Premier League.

A large part of that success was the partnerships he created all over the pitch, with the most notorious being between Heung-Min Son and Harry Kane. The duo have combined for more Premier League goals than any other pairing in competition history, and most of those came under Pochettino's tutelage.

At Chelsea, Pochettino also managed to create a brilliant partnership between Cole Palmer and Nicolas Jackson to help the team qualify for the Champions League before he was rather harshly dismissed after just one campaign at Stamford Bridge.

Now the Argentine will be looking to do similar at Old Trafford, and it's clear that he already has the tools and personnel to at least replicate the South Korean superstar's skillset.

United's attacking options are strong. Bruno Fernandes is the talisman in the number ten role, while Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo, Amad, Joshua Zirkzee, and Benjamin Sesko provide experience and quality. Shea Lacey provides a wildcard out wide as a youngster, and is someone that Pochettino will love, while Mason Mount can be useful when he's fit.

But the forward who is likely to take the most joy from Pochettino's arrival is Marcus Rashford, and the manager can easily use him as the perfect Heung-Min Son clone in his team.

It was a surprise to see Rashford return to Man Utd in the summer following a successful loan spell at Barcelona, and he started the season well. He created a number of chances for teammates and looked sharp, even without registering a goal or assist.

But the England international hasn't featured since the 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid last month due to an ongoing hip issue, missing six games. Once he returns to fitness he will offer that same sharpness and direct running that Pochettino loves in his wingers, where he can hug the touchline, make runs from out to in, and punish teams.

He has the goal record to prove he is capable of being a gamechanger, too. With 138 goals for the club, nobody in the current squad has scored more, while the 30 goals he scored in the 2022/23 season are more than anyone else has ever managed in a single campaign at the club from the current squad.

That was a while ago, but at Barcelona he scored 14 goals and registered 14 assists last season, and he was in good form at the World Cup for England too, showing that he can deliver in the right setup. He was even described as 'frightening' by Ollie Watkins recently, showing how highly his teammates think of him.

"I can't speak highly enough of him," Watkins said on Rio Ferdinand Presents on YouTube.

"There was times (at Villa) where, like, I was on the bench, and he was keeping me out of the team, and I was frustrated, not because, not about him. It was just, I just wanted to play, but I could understand it, you know?

"There was times where, like, the PSG game, he absolutely ripped them apart. And I'm on the sideline, I'm thinking, I shouldn't come on there, really.

"Because he's, no, no, but I'm honest like that. Like, I don't have an ego. Like, I thought he was, because you read things and stuff like that, but I knew Marcus's talent, and I knew that the manager would get the best out of him. And to be fair, he did. And like, he was unbelievable. His ability is, yeah, it's frightening."

Pochettino will love what he can bring to the side, and he will love being trusted and relied upon. That could be the difference between getting him back to his best, and getting Man Utd back to where they feel they belong.

#1297. Official: D’Aversa replaces Aquilani at Sassuolo

Sassuolo have appointed Roberto D’Aversa as head coach following the dismissal of Alberto Aquilani.

According to an official club statement, the former Torino and Parma coach has signed a contract until 30 June 2027 and will take charge of his first training session this afternoon.

“U.S. Sassuolo Calcio announces that it has entrusted the technical leadership of the First Team to Roberto D’Aversa until 30 June 2027,” the statement read.

D’Aversa will be assisted by Salvatore Sullo, and he will be presented to the media at the Mapei Football Center on Thursday at 12:30 CET [11:30 GMT].

Aquilani was appointed in June for his first Serie A job, but he paid the price for a dismal run. Sassuolo have taken one point from their last seven games, conceding 29 goals so far this season, and Saturday’s 3-0 defeat at Roma left them 17th, only one point above the relegation zone.

D’Aversa knows all about relegation battles. He replaced Marco Baroni at Torino in February and turned their season around before leaving in the summer, when Ignazio Abate took over. He’s best known for taking Parma from Serie C to Serie A in consecutive seasons.

His first game in charge will be after the international break.

#1296. Trafford shows he has credentials to dislodge Pickford as England No 1

Has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

After leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

This was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

Goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

The first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

The second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

“It’s a positive [point],” said Le Bris. “The more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.”

“It’s a positive [point], the more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.

Leeds make the next change as Nmecha replaces Calvert-Lewin up top. Trafford collides with Muharemovic as he comes out to claim a cross. He initially stays down and it looks like he has cramp, but he’s okay to continue and play resumes.

Bogle bursts forward on the right flank and fires a powerful, teasing cross towards the back post. Okafor makes the run, but Sadiki is there to make a terrific interception and clear the danger.

Bogle catches Reinildo above his hip with a high boot. The referee gives the Leeds man a yellow card. Sunderland want something more. That was certainly a risky tackle from Bogle, who now must be careful.

Let's go, Timur 👊 https://t.co/JVxgPM7zAC

Attacking changes are here for both sides. Brobbey’s Sunderland return lasts for over an hour and he’s replaced by Tutierov. Meanwhile, for the visitors, Wilson and Aaronson depart for Stach and Okafor.

Bogle carelessly catches Angulo with a late tackle, gifting Sunderland a great chance to swing the ball into the box. Le Fee whips it in, but its flicked on and goes out for a goal kick.

This game is now being played at a much quicker tempo, with Justin bending an effort towards the far top corner. However, it drifts wide. Both sides look far more confident now and not like they’re playing for a draw.

At the other end, the ball breaks to Angulo, who stings Trafford’s palms with a fierce curling strike that forces the Leeds goalkeeper into conceding a corner. Excitement in this second half is starting to ramp up.

Leeds come forward again as Bogle tries to slide a low cross into Tanaka, but Le Fee tracks back to prevent the visitors from getting a shot off.

Wilson whips in a deep corner. Muharemovic wins the header at the back stick, but can’t get threatening contact on it and slowly directs it into Roefs’ grasp.

If I’m being kind to the players out there, playing in a strong wind at the Stadium of Light is notoriously tricky.

If you are watching on television, you might have noticed in the first half the litter being blown around in circles on the pitch. That will give you an idea of the conditions. The wind tends to swirl around inside this stadium rather than blowing in one direction. If I were any good at physics I would be able to tell you why. But I’m not. So I can’t.

Still, this match is yet to strike an attacking rhythm. Leeds have dominated the ball since the break, with Mukiele’s injury and subsequent departure slightly unsettling the hosts. Aaronson acrobatically knocks the ball across the six-yard box, but it’s hooked clear by Sunderland.

Mukiele won’t return to the action and heads down the tunnel. Alderete is on to replace his fellow defender. That is a blow for Sunderland to lose Mukiele this early in the second half.

We're forced into a change 🔄 https://t.co/ZJB0NOnawt

Mukiele is sat up and is still receiving treatment after being caught by O’Nein on his Adam’s apple. He walks off the pitch and it’s unclear if he’s able to continue. For now, Sunderland are down to 10 men.

The medical staff are waved on to the pitch as O’Nein accidentally catches Mukiele in the face with his outstretched arm.

We are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break.

Only two shots on target in that first half, with Brobbey forcing a couple of saves from Trafford. Hopefully we’re treated to some more exciting football after the break.

In a game lacking creativity and chances, nothing separates Sunderland and Leeds at the break. The best chance of the first half fell to Brobbey, but Trafford did well to smother the one-on-one opportunity.

There will be just one minute of added time to end this first half.

Nearly a disaster at the back for Sunderland as O’Nein lets a ball run thinking Roefs will come out to clear. However, the goalkeeper stays put. With Calvert-Lewin closing in, O’Nein has to make a last-ditch sliding challenge to direct the ball back to Roefs to stop the striker in his tracks.

Reinildo is booked as Bogle turns him, with the Sunderland defender dragging the Leeds man to the florr. He protests his innocence, and in fairness to Reinildo, he has a ripped shirt. He must be freezing.

Hume draws huge applause from the home fans as he crunches into a challenge on Gudmundsson. The Sunderland fans loved that sliding tackle.

Leeds are still waiting to record a shot on target. They’ve been pretty safe and unadventurous in forward areas so far.

A lot of huff and puff, honest endeavour and robust challenges in this game so far, but the two moments of quality have come from Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford. His first save to deny Brian Brobbey was excellent. He perfectly judged the trajectory of an awkward bouncing ball at full stretch, but I think the second is even better.

Trafford was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international but the way he stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb. He may have saved with his feet, but he cramped Brobbey for room and timed his moment to dive at his feet perfectly. That was elite level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Ampadu picks up the game’s first yellow card for bumping into Angulo on the edge of his own box. Sunderland now have a free kick in a promising position. Unfortunately for the hosts, Le Fee smacks it straight into the wall.

Sunderland’s pressure nearly pays off as Xhaka forces Wilson into a mistake. Brobbey is then too strong for Bijol and shrugs the defender off the ball. From a tight angle, the striker has a one-on-one opportunity against Trafford, but the Leeds goalkeeper does well to block Brobbey’s side-footed effort.

Sunderland fans are urging their side to press at every opportunity, cheering each time an intervention is successful. Still, we wait for the first notable chance.

Mukiele is down after being caught in the face by Calvert-Lewin as they both challenged for a high ball. There was no malice in the striker’s attempt to win possession and play swiftly continues following some quick treatment for Mukiele.

Mukiele was gearing up for a long throw, but the Sunderland defender held onto the ball for too long, with referee Attwell sounding his whistle to give possession back to Leeds.

Ampadu’s long throw-in casuses some momentary chaos in Sunderland’s six-yard box. However, the linesman’s flag is raised and Leeds’ chance disappears.

It’s been a scrappy opening to this game. Mukiele tries a very ambitious effort from long range, but he drags the shot well wide and it harmlessly trickles out of play.

O’Nein defends unconvincingly as he battles with Calvert-Lewin and attempts to deal with a long ball. The centre back just about handles the situation and prevents the striker from carving out a one-on-one opportunity.

On his return to the Sunderland line-up, Brobbey tests Trafford in Sunderland’s first attack. The striker’s deflected effort bounces awkwardly in front of the goalkeeper, who parries the ball out for a corner. Leeds then defend the set-piece well and clear the danger.

That was a deceptively hard save for James Trafford to make to deny Brian Brobbey. Although the connection was not the cleanest, that almost made it harder as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the England international meant he had to watch it all the way and keep a strong hand at full stretch. Excellent work from the summer signing from Manchester City.

Leeds are dominating the ball in these early exchanges. Sunderland look slightly unsettled so far. Bogle is pushing particularly far forward for the visitors.

Wilson starts for Leeds. The Welshman was pivotal for Fulham last season. His Leeds career is yet to meaningfully get going, but he has a great chance to impress today.

Leeds get us under way here. How will come out on top in these feisty northern weather conditions?

My favourite part of every Sunderland game is the singing of Elvis Presley’ Can’t Help Falling in Love before kick off. Not sure the “The King” had a football club on Wearside in mind when he wrote it but it just works as a pre-match anthem. I also grew up in a house where there was a lot of Elivs playing when I was a small child. Anyway, on to the football.

The Stadium of Light is in fantastic spirits as per usual, despite Sunderland floundering in 20th position. Can the home side record a much-needed win to ignite their domestic season?

Starting good in the season, we are really keen to follow our goals for our system where we train every week and we follow how our team should play.

And, how the XI plus the subs should play together, fight for each other, and we have to keep on going like this. We know how good Sunderland are.

The team is good. Obviously, every team has a different start in the season but still we know what this team can do. Last year they achieved Europe so it is a really big thing.

We know the players and, yeah, we know how hard these games can be but we are here to try to win and to take all the points.

It is going to be a tough one. Also, the weather, I think. The wind is unbelievable but we are ready. We are here and ready to fight.

We go into every game confident and ready to fight for the three points. We are here to win. We are going for every game [because] we want to win so we will try our best and fight.

Right now, I think his intensity against the ball, his workload against the ball, is on a way better level in comparison to how it was when he arrived and as soon as he adapts, I’m pretty sure his quality will shine through sooner rather than later.

Leeds are always a good side, it was in the Championship and now in the Premier League.

They are doing really well, they are consistent as well. They built momentum early in the season, which is always good, so they are in a different position but anything is possible in football. We think that it is going to be a new opportunity to get better.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

The return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Sunderland: Roefs, Hume, Mukiele, O’Nien, Reinildo, Xhaka, Sadiki, Le Fée, Rigg, Angulo, BrobbeySubs: Ellborg, Methalie, Alderete, Diarra, Ahoka, Talbi, Fofana, Angulo, Tuterov

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

Following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”

#1295. Carbon radical generation by irreversible metal-to-ligand charge transfer

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) is a fundamental photoinduced process that underpins a broad range of energy- or electron-transfer events1,2. In the absence of productive substrate engagement, the MLCT excited state typically relaxes to the ground state via photophysical deactivation, reflecting its largely reversible character3,4. Here we report a class of isolable copper–heteroaryl sulfone complexes that, upon visible light irradiation, undergo an irreversible MLCT-driven fragmentation through C–S bond cleavage within the coordinated sulfone ligand, generating carbon-centered radicals. Spectroscopic and computational studies support the formation of MLCT-derived excited states and a low-barrier pathway for C–S bond cleavage. This reactivity is largely independent of the reduction potentials of the corresponding free sulfones, enabling the generation of fluoroalkyl and non-fluorinated tertiary, secondary, and primary (even methyl) alkyl radicals. We demonstrate the utility of this platform in copper-catalyzed C–H fluoroalkylation of arenes and terminal alkynes. Leveraging these MLCT-generated trifluoromethyl radicals to initiate halogen-atom transfer (XAT) from perfluorocyclobutyl iodide (I-FCB), we also achieve radical perfluorocyclobutylation–iodination of alkenes, addressing a longstanding challenge in the incorporation of perfluorocyclobutyl motifs.

#1294. Barcelona left-back Balde wanted by Roma and Juventus

Roma have added Barcelona left-back Alejandro Balde to their list of January targets, but they could face competition from Juventus.

According to TuttoMercatoWeb, the Catalan club are open to selling the 23-year-old in the winter window to raise funds for a new centre-back, which is Hansi Flick’s top priority for the second half of the season.

Roma have established themselves as genuine title contenders. They’re unbeaten after 11 games and two points off the top, and sporting director Tony D’Amico wants to strengthen Gian Piero Gasperini’s squad in January. Gasperini likes the Spain international, but a deal won’t be easy.

Balde’s valuation is high and so are his wages, so Roma would need to find the right formula. One option could be a loan with an obligation to buy, possibly linked to Champions League qualification.

There’s also plenty of competition. Liverpool, Aston Villa, Manchester United, Manchester City and Tottenham are all interested, as are Monaco. Juventus are also monitoring the situation because Andrea Cambiaso could leave.

#1293. Alisson, 34, reveals he wants to STAY at Liverpool after rolling back the years against Crystal Palace... but is extending the goalkeeper's contract the right call, asks LEWIS STEELE

Published: 07:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 13:09 EST, 10 November 2026

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker insists he wants to stay at the club after his contract expires at the end of this season.

The Brazilian, now 34, put in a throwback performance in the Reds’ win at Crystal Palace on Sunday with some fine stops to keep his side in the game at 0-0 before the big-money attackers did their job at the other end.

It came after a period where Alisson has been questioned by fans for a string of errors in what is his final contracted year at the club. And the No1 has now opened up on his future for the first time.

Asked if he wants to stay beyond the end of the season, Alisson said: ‘Yes, in my mind. I’m focused on playing every game but in my mind I’m happy to stay. You know, that depends on a lot of aspects and different situations.

‘But my will is to stay. I’m happy here, my family is happy here. I’m still hungry for titles and for delivering good performances. I still want to play at the top level for as long as I can. So that’s my thinking on that.’

Alisson later added that his agent has held talks with the club over a new deal.

The 34-year-old keeper will spend the next week resting after not being called up by Brazil for the second straight international window

The keeper will spend the next week resting after not being called up by Brazil for the second straight international window, which he admits is a decision taken somewhat beyond his will.

He said: ‘It is beneficial (not going), for sure. You have to use it right because you have a lot of time so if you don’t train, if you don’t prepare, time goes really quick and you need to stay sharp.

‘It’s not that I will sit on the couch for a week and then come back training. I still have to work hard but in my mind I can use the time to relax and be more with my family.

‘It’s a little bit against my will. What I always want is to be with the national team but I understand this is what I have at the moment and I will use this time and take the benefit from the rest.’

Should Liverpool continue in Alisson wonderland?

It is tempting to just say ‘yes’ and end this debate there.

Alisson is still the best goalkeeper Liverpool have on their books and, even though he is maybe not as solid as he once was, the 34-year-old remains one of the best goalkeepers in the world.

Last summer, he flirted with the idea of leaving and seriously considered a move to Juventus. Alisson speaks fluent Italian from his time at AS Roma and held talks with the Turin club over a return.

But Liverpool triggered a clause in his deal to extend his stay by a year. With several big names leaving such as Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson, Ibrahima Konate and Curtis Jones, the club did not want another experienced head to depart and leave a leadership vacuum.

They have also spent the last three years succession planning for Alisson’s long-term replacement and have signed a number of goalkeepers for more than £60million combined.

Giorgi Mamardashvili is the most obvious in the pecking order. He has had mixed reviews with fans but the Georgian is appreciated more internally than maybe externally. The club believes he has several levels left to step up.

Lucca Brughmans will join from Belgian side Genk after a £28.3million deal was struck. Liverpool genuinely think he is the best goalkeeper on the market and they fought off stiff competition from Real Madrid to sign him.

Liverpool think Lucca Brughmans - who will join them from Belgian side Genk - is the best goalkeeper on the market and they fought off stiff competition from Real Madrid to sign him

They have also signed highly-rated Armin Pecsi and England youth goalkeeper Zach Trinder from Wolves.

Clearly, the post-Alisson future is sorted, with some of them tipped to go far in the game. But are any of them better than Alisson now? No. Will any of them be better next season? No.

Alisson missed 54 games across the previous two seasons with injury and illness, according to Transfermarkt, but his omission from Brazil camps and a specialised pre-season programme mean the keeper seems to have put his issues behind him. Touch wood.

For that reason, a one-year extension makes sense – for both Alisson and 35-year-old captain Virgil van Dijk. The club will have to face up to a future without both of their defensive stalwarts but, for now, they remain the best in class.
